title: Pogačar's sensational solo attack squeezes Vuelta rivals dry
text:
Four days is all it took for Tadej Pogačar to end the Vuelta a España as a meaningful contest, the Slovenian great once more riding away from the peloton to win solo and establish a massive lead over the rest of the field.

It has been 32 years since Tony Rominger led a grand tour from start to finish when he won the 1994 Vuelta.

But with yet another thrilling display of daring, Pogačar put himself in pole position to emulate the Swiss rider and become just the ninth man to lead a three-week race from start to finish.

Superlatives have long been superfluous when writing about this Slovenian superstar.

Things that should not be possible are made to look routine.

When he hits the front of a race as the road goes into the mountains, the rest of the pack knows that their only chance is to ride their own tempo.

Any attempt to fly too close to this generation's greatest star will surely result in an Icarus tragedy to their hopes of finishing the race.

As soon as Tadej Pogačar is in this position, that's likely to be the last the peloton sees of him. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Pogačar took off with just over 50 kilometres remaining of the 104.8km circuit around Andorra la Vella to claim yet another dominant victory.

Decathlon CMA CGM put the power down on the bottom of the Collada de Beixalis climb, the second mountain of the day, and ripped the peloton to shreds.

Australian Jay Vine led the charge in support for the Slovenian's UAE Emirates XRG team, but with the pace already high, Pogačar simply upped his rate to burst clear.

Decathlon's Austrian leader Felix Gall tried to match Pogačar's pace in the initial throes of his attack.

However, the Austrian, as so many riders have discovered before him, could barely hold the double-world champion's wheel and quickly dropped off before being joined by the rest of the favourites.

"The pace was already super fast on the throttle right from the base [of the climb]," Pogačar told media after the race.

"When Jay let me pass him on Decathlon's wheel, I knew: 'OK, I don't want to get isolated from all those general classification contenders, because otherwise they'll all gang up on me.'

"I tried to attack on the climb. When I saw that I could open up a gap, I just hoped I could hold on until the finish. It worked out.

"It was really tough, but it's a wonderful feeling."

Tadej Pogačar is irresistable. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Pogačar's lead extended out to over 3 minutes at one stage before he rolled home to win by 2 minutes and 39 seconds from Jarno Widar, with Gall third.

The 50km attack was his longest in a grand tour, bettering the 43km solo victory he launched in the Pyrenees last month at the Tour de France.

It is another remarkable performance from the Slovenian to add to the extraordinary wins that have become so normalised that it is almost expected of him.

Why these people believe in 'freak' Tadej Pogačar's victories As Tadej Pogačar continues to mop up cycling's biggest accolades and most controversial record, one former doper believes he's found the answer to his success: he is just a "freak".

With two key objectives to come this season, the World Championships road race in Canada falls just two weeks after the Vuelta's conclusion, with the Giro di Lombardia a further two weeks after that, Pogačar may now be able to take things easier through the next two-and-a-half weeks of racing in Spain.

The 27-year-old's lead in the general classification now stands at 3 minutes and 21 seconds, with four-time Vuelta winner Primož Roglič sitting second.

"To be honest, any lead is a bonus," Pogačar said.

"This is fantastic, because now I can head into the coming days with peace of mind and a lot of confidence.

"We're taking it day by day and staying focused. Hopefully, after this stage, the pressure will ease up a bit."

Pogačar is also a comprehensive leader in the points and king of the mountains classifications.

Wednesday's fifth stage is a hilly 173.3km ride from Falset Costa Datura to Terres de l'Ebre in Spain's north east.

title: Fares secretly hiked to fund Suburban Rail Loop, auditor-general finds
text:
Public transport fares were secretly raised last year to help fund the Suburban Rail Loop, which is likely to be delivered late and over budget, the Victorian Auditor-General's Office (VAGO) has found.

New Premier Ben Carroll on Tuesday declared he would find $2 billion worth of savings on SRL East, the first leg of the mega project, and that it would be delivered on time and under budget.

But this has been immediately challenged by an audit of the SRL East delivery, revealing the state government had introduced a secret levy on public transport fares to help fill the funding gap.

The government wants to fund one-third of the project — which has been cut from $34.5 billion to $33.3 billion, with a further $1 billion saving expected — through taxes and charges known as value capture.

The VAGO on Wednesday said the government never revealed this included a new levy on public transport fares from the start of 2025.

The 1 per cent increase was hidden in the annual increase to ticket costs with inflation.

"The government plans to allocate 60 per cent of the revenue it collects through the levy, estimated at $4.8 billion in net present value (NPV) terms to 2062, to fund SRL East," the report said.

" This levy will be the project's largest source of value capture revenue. "

The government plans for trains to start running on the Suburban Rail Loop by 2035. (Supplied: Victoria's Big Build)

This was approved in August 2021, when Mr Carroll was public transport minister. Public transport is half-price this year.

"The government and Transport Victoria did not acknowledge the levy in their public communications about the 2025 and 2026 annual fare increases."

Treasurer Colin Brooks today denied the levy, which has so far raised $6.5 million, was going towards the SRL project directly.

"It's not part of the value capture framework for SRL … it is going directly into public transport," he said.

But he conceded the government should have been more transparent.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said: "Labor's secret public transport tax is a scandal of the highest order.

"Ben Carroll was the minister for public transport when this secret tax was approved in 2021," she said.

"What other secret taxes are Labor levying on Victorians without telling them?"

SRL East likely 'exceed publicly disclosed cost', VAGO finds

Mr Carroll this week announced $1 billion in immediate savings to SRL East by removing "nice to haves" such as pedestrian bridges and underground interchanges, and announced a review to find a further $1 billion in cuts.

This would bring the total estimated investment down from $34.5 billion to around $32 billion.

The premier said further contracts would not be signed until that review was completed, likely after the election.

But the VAGO report said the procurement process to build six stations had been delayed by around one year.

"The project has experienced significant delays," it said.

An early works package was also finished six months late.

SRL East is "more likely than not to exceed its publicly disclosed cost", the report said.

Soil contamination, higher than expected market costs, and delays because of government decisions to slow spending on the project to manage debt had all helped push up the cost.

Victoria hopes to get one-third of the cost from the Commonwealth, which has so far committed $6 billion.

Report comes amid budget pressure, job cuts

The VAGO report comes amid news the Victorian Government will cut 140 public sector jobs a bid to bring the budget under control, as the premier continues a campaign of fiscal responsibility.

The jobs will be axed from executive roles across government departments, including the Suburban Rail Loop Authority (SRLA) and the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (VIDA).

It adds to 332 executive roles already earmarked for redundancy by the government and expected to be cut by early 2027.

Treasurer Colin Brooks said while public servants were hard-working, it was a necessary decision to keep the state's balances in the black.

"This is a difficult decision but an important decision to reduce the number of senior public servants to free up budget capacity to provide the very important services that Victorians rely on," Mr Brooks said.

Mr Brooks said the last figures he had seen in mid-2025 put the number of executive staff at more than 1,900.

"The growth in that number is something we need to address to maintain our budget surplus," he said.

Treasurer Colin Brooks conceded the executive workforce had grown to unsustainable levels and needed reducing. (AAP: Diego Fedele)

When asked why the government had allowed the executive workforce to balloon out to unsustainable levels, Mr Brooks had no answer and said he had only been the treasurer for four weeks.

Mr Brooks said the government would also be seeking $12 million in savings from parliament, which has previously been exempt from cost-cutting measures.

Today's announced cuts come after widespread job cuts last year that saw "thousands" of public sector roles cut, according to then-premier Jacinta Allan.

The government said those cuts, triggered by an independent review of inefficiencies in the Victorian public sector, would save $4 billion over four years.

The report, prepared by independent reviewer Helen Silver, found the public workforce has ballooned since the COVID-19 pandemic and needed significant reductions.

The Victorian public sector review found the state had more than 3,400 boards and committees and 500 public entities, with an annual operating expenditure of more than $35 billion.

title: Ex-NBA player who claims to be a woman banned by WNBA team after joust
text:
The Chicago Sky has banned Enes Kanter Freedom from its home games after the former NBA centre was ejected from Sunday's (Monday AEST) loss to the Indiana Fever.

Owner Michael Alter made the announcement at a rare news conference on Tuesday, local time. Alter told reporters Kanter Freedom is not allowed inside Wintrust Arena for Sky games "unless sometime in the future, he's able to prove to us that he's able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat".

Kanter Freedom was removed from Sunday's game after a confrontation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt Sophie Cunningham insists she wants to protect the sanctity of women's sport, but her comments have opened her league up to an unprecedented attack.

Kanter Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female".

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then chest-bumped teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning and walking in Kanter Freedom's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter Freedom, 34, as she approached him. Kanter Freedom, who was standing, held his arms out and stepped onto the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved between the two.

"It was pretty clear to us that his purpose of coming here was trying to be provocative and see how much attention he could get," Alter told reporters from the Chicago Sun-Times and other media outlets.

Kanter Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing the arena.

"I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!" Kanter Freedom wrote on social media. "Let that sink in, AMERICA!"

Kanter Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women. But a person familiar with the decision told the AP on Monday, local time, that they are not eligible. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the situation.

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

AP

title: How Dolly Parton fostered child literacy as a tribute to her dad
text:
While Dolly Parton was known as the Queen of Country, her work improving child literacy rates will be another of her lasting legacies.

Parton, who died this week aged 80, grew up in extreme poverty in the Great Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee, the fourth of 12 children to her parents Robert Lee and Avie Lee Parton.

Parton adored her dad, describing him as "the smartest man I've ever known" with a good head for numbers.

However, he never learned to read or write after leaving school at a young age to work to help support his family.

"I knew in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from seeing all his dreams come true," Parton said on social media.

"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."

Her tribute to her dad became the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, which she established in1995, initially to help underprivileged kids in her rural home county.

"When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee I knew my dreams would come true," Parton wrote on the organisation's website.

"I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.

" The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world. "

It has now been operating for 31 years, expanding across the US, the UK, Ireland, Canada and Australia, where it was established in 2013.

How does it work?

Every month the Imagination Library sends an age-appropriate book to all registered children at no cost to their family.

Kids can register from birth, and receive a monthly book until the age of five.

Dolly Parton at the launch of her Imagination Library of the United Kingdom. (Getty: Yui Mok)

The program has so far gifted 332 million books to children around the world.

More than 2 million of those books have gone to kids in Australia.

Australia's selection committee, which is run by United Way Australia and is comprised of early education and literacy experts, picks titles specific to the region, and includes Indigenous writers and publishing organisations.

Previous book selections have included the board book Australian Babies, With Sky Country by Annette Sax, Backyard Footy by Carl Merrison and Pamela Allen's Who Sank the Boat?

The program has been embraced by public libraries around the country.

Loading...

Its effect on literacy

The Imagination Library's impact has been far-reaching and affirmed in an international study led by United Way Australia's head of research, statistician Claire Galea, in 2025.

The study, which is the largest dataset in the world on shared book reading, collected data from 86,000 families with children in the program.

It found in all countries, the program significantly helped prevent early literacy gaps that often persisted in primary school.

Children enrolled in Imagination Library were also nine times more likely to be read to four or more days per week compared to those not in the program.

In Australia, the number one benefit reported by caregivers was seeing their children develop a strong love of books and reading.

Dr Galea's thesis specifically looked at the impact of the program in Tamworth, finding children in this local government area were read to more often, for longer, and had more books in the home than the average Australian child.

The Imagination Library team posted a tribute to Parton on social media, saying they were "heartbroken at the loss of our founder".

" The work ahead has never felt more meaningful, and we will carry it forward as she lifts us all up. Dolly, we will always love you. "

title: Gulf trucking company halt could force remote grocery price surge
text:
The price of food in Queensland's most remote communities could cost "an arm and a leg" as a major trucking company is grounded to address compliance issues.

Hawkins Transport runs 70 road trains across the Gulf of Carpentaria, delivering cattle and taking about 60 pallets of groceries a week to remote Indigenous communities including Kowanyama and Doomadgee.

Earlier this month, the Normanton-based business was issued a prohibition from the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator (NHVR), which grounded its entire fleet.

A prohibition stops the company from operating its fleet and is considered a last resort from the regulator after a pattern of non-compliance, or if the body views the company as an imminent risk to public safety.

Doomadgee mayor Fred O'Keefe said the regulator did not understand the reality of living remotely.

Fred O'Keefe says finding an alternate supplier would be expensive and difficult. (Supplied: Doomadgee Aboriginal Shire Council)

"It's very, very difficult [to find drivers]," Cr O'Keefe said.

"If we get a trucking company from Brisbane, they wouldn't know where Doomadgee is until they get here."

As one of two major food transporters in the area, Cr O'Keefe said deliveries from an alternative supplier from Brisbane would incur a hefty premium.

"It will change the price, there's no two ways about it … we know we're going to hit with a higher freight cost if it's going to come out of Brisbane," he said.

"We are going to be paying an arm and a leg.

"Most of our people here are on unemployment … it's not going to cover their cost for their food, for their household."

Fred O'Keefe says local grocery prices would likely increase if a new supplier were to take over from Hawkins Transport. (ABC Brisbane: Allyson Horn, file photo)

'Half a million dollars a week'

Starting as a cattle transporter in 1998, Hawkins has steadily diversified into grocery and other freight, now employing more than 70 staff across Queensland's top end.

Owner Bradley Hawkins said issues with the regulator started about three years ago, with an audit revealing several defects such as oil leaks, dirty windscreens and a worn tyre needing to be replaced.

Mr Hawkins blamed poor literacy, staffing shortages and misunderstood reporting requirements for missed mandatory inspections, which led to the prohibition order.

"It's not like we just did not turn up. There was always an email trail," he said.

"It was a bit spasmodic because of the loss of different staff members … it's no excuse, but it's just what it is."

Mr Hawkins said he feared the prohibition could close the business.

"It's costing me half a million dollars a week," he said.

"If not [fixed] in two or three weeks, I'd have to consider some drastic moves."

Hawkins Transport has diversified since its opening in 1998. (Supplied: Hawkins Transport)

To lift the prohibition, Hawkins Transport is required to send its entire fleet for inspection at the nearest NHVR site, which is at Mount Isa, about 500 kilometres away.

Mr Hawkins agreed safety was a priority.

But the 10-hour round trip to Mount Isa and limited availability for inspections had been challenging.

"I asked them [NHVR] could they please work with me, it's [Normanton] a long way from anywhere, out in the middle of nowhere," Mr Hawkins said.

Mr Hawkins said it had taken a week for the regulator to start inspecting the company's gear once a prohibition was imposed.

"If they call this working with me, I'd hate to see if they're working against me," he said.

A NHVR spokesperson said the decision to impose a prohibition was carefully considered. (Supplied: Hawkins Transport)

In a statement, a NHVR spokesperson said the decision to impose a prohibition was not made lightly and was weighed against the impact it would have on remote communities.

"Prohibition notices seek to ensure that an activity that presents an immediate or imminent risk ceases at once, and that the activity does not resume until the recipient has remedied the risk in accordance with the notice," they said.

"Geography or the nature of the freight task does not change an operator's obligation to ensure its vehicles are safe and comply with the Heavy Vehicle National Law — the safety of those travelling on our roads always takes precedence."

Hawkins Transport has applied for a stay of the prohibition and will appear in Brisbane Supreme Court tomorrow to contest the matter.

title: Victorian offshore wind auction opens with plans to power 1.5 million homes
text:
The Victorian government has opened its first offshore wind auction, inviting companies to bid to supply the first 2 gigawatts (GW) of power to the grid.

The auction is expected to deliver enough electricity to power 1.5 million homes each year and create thousands of jobs.

Successful applicants will receive government support to deliver their projects.

Victoria is home to Australia's first declared offshore wind zone in waters off the Gippsland coast and another off the state's south west coast near Warrnambool.

Bidding in the auction is now open and will close in August next year.

The Victorian government said it expects to award contracts in 2028, allowing successful projects to move towards securing investment, construction and operation.

The auction was planned last year, but was delayed while the state and federal governments worked on the timing.

The first offshore wind is not expected to enter the grid until 2035, seven years after the closure of the Yallourn coal plant in the Latrobe Valley.

Last year Yallourn provided 14.8 per cent of Victoria's power.

Victorian Energy Minister Jaclyn Symes said offshore wind was an "amazing opportunity" for Victoria which would produce cheap, reliable power and deliver thousands of jobs, particularly in Gippsland.

"Offshore wind is a very important component of our future way to create energy as coal retires," Ms Symes said.

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) has indicated that demand for electricity was exploding due to the growth in data centres, which it forecast would draw as much power as all homes in Victoria and New South Wales by 2036.

But Ms Symes said AEMO had indicated that Victoria would not face a shortfall when Yallourn closes.

The government planned to award contracts through the Electricity Services Entry Mechanism (ESEM), a scheme to drive investment in the sector.

The ESEM was agreed in principle late last year by energy ministers across Australia, with the exception of Queensland, and is yet to be adopted.

The government will assess bidders based on their value for money and ability to deliver benefits for local communities.

Victoria has a target to produce at least 2 GW of power from offshore wind by 2032, increasing to 4 GW in 2035 and 9 GW in 2040.

Auction welcomed by industry

Offshore wind developer Southerly Ten has welcomed the opening of the auction, saying it was "really good news" for the industry.

"It's really the signal that government is looking to bring offshore wind into the market and we know that's really important as some of the coal plants start to retire over the coming decade," chief development officer Erin Coldham said.

"One of the things that's really critical to make sure that offshore wind projects can proceed is to have that partnership with government through these types of contracts."

Southerly Ten is the developer of the 2.2 gigawatt (GW) Star of the South, which is Australia's most advanced offshore wind project.

Ms Coldham said the company would review the auction documents in anticipation of bidding.

"We've been working very hard over a number of years to get all of the approvals ready, and this is really the next step for us to participate in this process, see what the government is seeking and take the project forward from there," she said.

title: CTE study finds 70pc of head impacts happening in sports practice
text:
At least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), according to a new study.

Out of the 878 former players who died during that timeframe 235 donated their brains, researchers said, with 215 of those donated brains found to have CTE.

The study's lead author Daniel Daneshvar, the chair of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said it was difficult to determine how common CTE was as it could only be diagnosed after death.

"People who donate their brains are more likely to donate if they have some concern, some reason for donating, if they think that either they or a loved one is having problems with their memory or thinking or concentration or behaviour changes," he told ABC News Breakfast.

Former NFL players donated their brains to the study and 215 out of 235 were found to have CTE. (Getty Images: Nic Antaya)

"And so you can't just look at the rate of CTE amongst people who donate to get a sense of how common this disease is."

Dr Daneshvar said the "possible prevalence of CTE" among NFL players was "very concerning".

"In the general population, less than 1 per cent of people get this disease pathology in their brain," he said.

" What we found is, at a minimum, 25 per cent of these NFL players died with this disease process. "

The study from Mass General Brigham, Boston University, and the Concussion & CTE Foundation also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures that focus on cutting down on repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport.

"Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," Dr Daneshvar said.

"The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn't occur at the NFL level.

Here's what we know about CTE The brain disease is caused by repeated head injuries. It's most commonly associated with athletes in contact sports, but there's a lot researchers are still trying to learn about it.

"They occurred at the collegiate level ... and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level.

" And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk. "

The NFL's 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement limited the number of contact practices during the season. The Ivy League banned full-contact tackling during practices five years later.

The Supreme Court cleared the way for the NFL's settlement of concussion-related lawsuits with thousands of retired players in 2016.

An NFL spokesperson said the league continuously strives to make the game of football safer, "including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts".

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental wellbeing," they said.

"We encourage former players to utilise these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."

Dr Daneshvar urged current and former athletes experiencing cognitive symptoms to seek a neurodegenerative disease expert evaluation.

"If the changes that have been implemented at the NFL level, including reducing the amount of contact in sports practices to less than one per week, were propagated at the collegiate, high school, and youth levels, athletes would be better off," he said.

"We know that nearly 70 per cent of head impacts are occurring in practice.

"So without changing a single minute of game time at any of those levels, we can be substantially reducing the cumulative head impact burden that these individuals are experiencing throughout their lives."

ABC/Reuters

title: Councils criticise how Victoria plans to divvy up $140m to Murray-Darling Basin towns
text:
Victoria is finalising plans to carve up $140 million for communities affected by water buybacks in the Murray-Darling Basin, despite pushback from seven councils over how the funding will be divvied up.

Victorian Water Minister Michaela Settle says the state's share of the Sustainable Communities Program (SCP) will be delivered after consultation with communities, including irrigators.

The Sustainable Communities Program is a federal initiative, providing $300 million over four years to minimise socio-economic impacts on basin communities as a result of water recovery measures.

It has already rolled out in New South Wales and South Australia, but has, to date, been off-limits to Victorians after the state's refusal to sign the Murray-Darling Basin voluntary water buybacks scheme.

Now, the Victorian government says it is negotiating with the Commonwealth to accept $140 million, despite its opposition to the "non-strategic buybacks".

Ms Settle said the allocation of funding would likely be split between Agriculture Victoria, state water projects and individual councils.

Funding 'can help' if done right

Last month, the Murray River Group of Councils — made up of six regional councils — and Greater Shepparton City Council called for the Victorian government to pause the funding and rethink its approach.

The group believes the proposed allocation of funding does not address the individuality of the regions affected by water buybacks.

Stuart King says council must have a seat at the table when it comes to planning the allocation of funds. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

The current plan for the councils' portion of the funding involves it being delivered through Regional Development Victoria (RDV), which group chair and Swan Hill Mayor Stuart King said adds "another layer of oversight".

The ABC has not been supplied a copy of the plan, but Cr King said only about $10 million of the $140 million was due to be allocated to RDV for distribution between councils.

Gannawarra Shire Mayor Garner Smith said he did not want the money to go to waste.

"There are already plans and strategies lining bookshelves gaining dust and there's no follow-up funding to even make them happen, even if they happen to contain some good ideas," he said.

" I think she's [the minister's] just totally missed the whole point. "

Cr King said funds should be allocated to local government directly so it can distribute funds in a way that accurately meets the needs of the community.

"Every one of our communities has been affected differently by water recovery. Each has its own industries, strengths and opportunities," he said.

"[Local government] knows where the opportunities exist, where the chances lie and what investments will deliver meaningful long-term economic and social benefits."

No plans to pause program

When asked if the funding allocation would be changed or postponed until after the state election, Ms Settle said, "Certainly not".

"I'm really keen to get that money out into the community," she said.

"We've had many conversations, the community wants to see that money on the ground and I'm working to get it out as soon as possible so that we can support farmers that are facing issues around their water and irrigation, we can support communities to stay strong through development."

Michaela Settle was appointed Victoria's water minister earlier this month. (ABC Ballarat: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Ms Settle acknowledged there were various views on how the money should be spent, but believed the government had "found the best way forward".

In NSW, councils, businesses, and organisations can apply for a share of $160 million, which is allocated across various grant rounds.

The same process applies in SA, where $20 million was given under the federal initiative.

Consultation with communities

Ms Settle said government had done an "enormous amount of consultation" with community, farmers, councils and local representatives, but Cr King said the councils felt they have not been included.

"We had preliminary meetings late last year in regards to this and we laid out some generic ideas … about how we thought that this funding could support and assist local government, and then we heard crickets," Cr King said.

SCP funding was previously unavailable to Victorians due to the state's refusal to sign the Murray-Darling Basin water buybacks scheme. (ABC Rural: Tom Nancarrow)

He said the group wrote to former water minister Harriet Shing before this month's cabinet reshuffle, as well as Ms Settle, with "no response".

"I came face-to-face with the minister at a function in Parliament House last week and reminded her of our request," he said.

"She was aware of it, but still no response."

Political motivations questioned

Last week, Ms Settle suggested political motivation may be involved in the councils' opposition to the program.

Cr Smith was this month announced as the One Nation's candidate for Murray Plains at the upcoming November election.

Garner Smith says his council was excluded from some parts of the planning process. (Supplied)

"We've also consulted a lot with the councils and to be frank, I was a little disappointed," Ms Settle said.

"One wonders if it's politically motivated to come out from the Gannawarra fellow [Cr Smith], because we have been speaking to them about this and we found a place where we can support farmers, we can support communities, and that's through irrigation projects, development projects, and also making sure communities stay strong."

In response, Cr Smith requested the minister meet with the group to discuss the matter.

"Let us discuss our concerns because right now, Gannawarra as a community is probably looking at getting $1 million out of the $150 million sustainable communities fund and I just don't think that's acceptable," he said.

"We've put in the request; she just has to approve it and the ball's in her court."

title: Tomic's main draw drought continues as Australians struggle at US Open
text:
Bernard Tomic's seemingly unending quest to fight his way back into another grand slam main draw has fallen short once again at Flushing Meadows despite one more worthy scrap from the veteran Australian.

The last time the 33-year-old managed to battle into a main draw of a major was at his home Australian Open in 2021.

In the five years since, he has entered 10 more qualifying events in the slams and failed to negotiate his way through any.

Alas for the former teenage wonder boy who got to number 17 in the world a decade ago, that drought continued on Tuesday afternoon, local time, in New York as he fought back in his first-round match against South African Lloyd Harris only to be outplayed in the final stanza.

No-one can possibly fault the effort of world number 179 Tomic, who was once perceived as being a talented but undisciplined figure who did not really care enough about the sport, as he has since battled on in the lower reaches of the game around the world, tirelessly seeking another day in the sun.

Emerson Jones also failed in her bid to advance to the women's main draw despite a valiant fight. (AAP: Darren England)

But Harris, a former world number 31 himself who is still dangerous even if his ranking has fallen to 139, just had a little too much for the Gold Coast veteran, who staged a second-set fightback before going down 6-2, 5-7, 6-2.

It was the same story for a couple of other Australians in first-round action, as teenager Emerson Jones fought valiantly to peg back Dutch world number 164 Suzan Lamens in a tight second-set tiebreak, only to succumb in the decider 7-5, 6-7 (7-9), 6-2 after two hours and 25 minutes.

With another veteran, Alex Bolt, losing 7-6 (7-3), 7-5 to Spain's Pablo Llamas Ruiz, it meant that Australia were still looking for their first winner of the week in qualifying after James McCabe's loss on the opening Monday.

At least one Aussie was guaranteed a place in the second round of qualifying as Storm Hunter took on her friend Maddison Inglis later in the day.

title: Imperfect lychees go from shed floor to liquor shelf as growers diversify
text:
Repeatedly seeing edible lychees discarded for their cosmetic imperfections has led central Queensland grower Krystal Caton on a mission to use the third-grade fruit.

"We were seeing waste from our lychees. Whilst it's only a small percentage, those lychees have already been harvested from the trees, so the expenses have already been spent," she said.

Ms Caton and her husband Paul are first-generation farmers with a 9,000-tree lychee orchard at South Yaamba, 30 minutes outside Rockhampton.

They have recently collaborated with a Yeppoon distillery to craft lychee-infused vodka and liqueur.

There are about 50 lychee orchards across Australia, along the east coast. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

The sweet fruit originated in southern China more than 2,000 years ago.

At the central Queensland farm, it is harvested over December and January and graded by quality, with the top produce sent to international and domestic markets.

The third-grade fruit was typically discarded, given to the cattle for feed or sent home with workers.

"Because they just [have] cosmetic damage on the outside of the fruit … inside of the fruit is perfectly fine," Ms Caton said.

Workers at the Lush Lychee farm in a previous season sorting the fruit. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

" We saw an opportunity and thought why not try developing that into another product? "

The shelf product also creates a way lychees can be enjoyed all year round.

"On top of the value add, because we're just a short season, it's also creating consumer continuity of awareness throughout the year … [and not having to] wait till next Christmas," Mr Caton said.

Exploring post-harvest opportunities for lychees has been a passion for Ms Caton and was the focus of her report as a 2025 Nuffield Scholar.

The Caton children pulling weeds during the off season over winter at the South Yaamba farm. (Supplied: Krystal Caton)

The coveted agriculture industry scholarship allowed her to travel overseas, study international lychee production and attend conferences.

Her research and findings will be presented later this year, with a focus on how family farms can value-add.

"Essentially utilising the assets that we already have here and seeing where else the value is being lost, and can we capture some of that in order to stay resilient, be more profitable, and grow our business," she said.

Paul and Krystal Caton with their new vodka and liqueur, crafted using lychees grown on their South Yaamba orchard. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Lychees, zucchini and finger limes

The lychee vodka and liqueur have been crafted at a Yeppoon distillery.

For the first batch, the Catons sent 80 kilograms of last season's leftover fruit that was frozen.

Laureth Rumble opened Reef Distillers in 2023 in Yeppoon on the Capricorn Coast. (Supplied: Reef Distillers)

"Lychees is such an amazing fruit to work with, so quintessential Queensland," Reef Distillers co-owner Laureth Rumble said.

Each bottle contains 14 lychees.

Alongside the lychee alcohol, Reef Distillers also works with other growers to value-add their product, including zucchini flowers from Ayr and finger limes from the Capricorn Coast.

"One of the things that really was important for our vision was to take ingredients that are on this Great Barrier Reef coastline and bring that into our spirits, collaborating with local farmers and growers," Ms Rumble said.

Botanicals mixed in the distilling process to create the Great Barrier dry gin. (Supplied: Reef Distillers)

The fruit is mixed with grain-based ethanol in the 500-litre still, affectionately named "Mr Bean".

"The vapours go through it and at the end, we infuse with the lychees, kind of like a tea bag," Ms Rumble explained.

The process to develop a new product takes about three to four months.

Transforming a lower-grade fruit into a high-value product was a win-win for growers, CQUni professor of regional economic development John Rolfe said.

John Rolfe says it is sensible for growers to spread their income streams. (Supplied: CQUni)

The horticulture industry is usually "saturated" during the season when the crops are harvested and everyone is selling at the same time.

"Transforming some of your product into value-added, it spreads your income stream, but it also reduces your risk on that supply at a particular week in the year, and the risk of price drop at that time," Professor Rolfe said.

Barriers to alcohol production in Australia

Alcohol production is not as common in Australia as elsewhere in the world, and in Queensland only a handful of lychee growers have turned their hand to it.

Professor Rolfe said while it was common in Europe to make schnapps out of apple and pear, in Australia it was much more industrialised and difficult to get liquor licenses.

"There's been some backyard hobbyists who make alcohol for their own use, or spirits for their own use, but commercially, I think it's fairly rare," he said.

" And that's in some ways to the grower's advantage, because then there's a real niche there that can be built. "

Professor Rolfe said the weather and infrastructure needed were some of the challenges.

"We have higher temperatures in Australia, so it's not as easy as in the cold countries to get the fermentation correct," he said.

"Scale is another issue here, generally producers have to produce, have large-scale operations, they've got to produce a lot of fruit to be viable."

The lychee trees have just come into flower at the Lush Lychees property, taken in August. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

But done well, it could bring wide-scale recognition for a region, Professor Rolfe explained.

He said consumers in metropolitan markets were often unaware of the product's origin.

"Whereas what is great in a regional setting is where we have producers who sell to local restaurants, local markets, local suppliers … so that the region becomes better known for its quality of produce," he said.

" If you have a number of producers that do that, you then end up with more of a food tourism culture in the region. "

title: Real estate agent's sales data under scrutiny after awards disqualification
text:
A real estate agent who took out the gong for being among Western Australia's top one per cent of agents has been disqualified from this year's annual industry awards after discrepancies emerged in his reported property sales data.

The Real Estate Institute of Western Australia (REIWA) provides price data on property transactions in the state, as well as allowing the public to view the prices fetched for properties listed and sold by its member agents.

Each year, agents win awards based on the total value and number of properties sold over the financial year.

Roy Li, whose legal name is Liang Li, a licensee and director of Ideal Realty WA, was last year in the top one per cent of performers by value of properties sold, an award category also dubbed the "grand master" agent category.

REIWA's website provides property sales information for its members in Western Australia. (ABC News: Rebecca Trigger)

But Mr Li has been disqualified from entering this year's awards due to the discrepancies in his data, while information he submitted for previous years could also be reviewed.

On Tuesday, the ABC revealed WA's Consumer Protection agency issued a warning to Ideal Realty after Mr Li allegedly used a shell company in 2024 to buy a home that he had been hired to sell.

He has denied the allegations, arguing he had disclosed his interest to the seller.

Price mismatch

Analysis by the ABC found that over the previous financial year, the sale price of at least one-third of the properties Mr Li listed with REIWA was not consistent with what was recorded on the state's official land title register.

The records also showed he had recorded the sales of six properties that either he or his Ideal Realty co-licensee Lin Ding owned, in transactions that added an additional almost $10 million to his sales tally for the year.

There were discrepancies in the sale prices Mr Li listed with REIWA. (ABC News: Benjamin Gubana)

At least two of these same properties appear to have been incorrectly listed as sold by them on two other major real estate websites in 2021 and again in 2024.

Mr Li said those properties had been withdrawn from the market, but due to an "administrative error" they were instead recorded as sold.

Following the ABC's queries, the sales records were removed from the REIWA website.

Historical sales data can influence the estimated value of a property on consumer real estate websites.

Mr Li acknowledged there were broader inaccuracies in his sales data.

Roy Li is a real estate agent based in Perth's southern suburbs. (ABC News: Rebecca Trigger)

"Ideal Realty recently identified errors in some historical sales-price entries, where advertised prices had been entered instead of the final prices recorded in accepted contracts," Mr Li said.

"Once the issue was identified, the records were reviewed and corrected information was provided to REIWA.

"We have also followed up with REIWA, as those changes are not yet reflected in its system."

REIWA says action being taken

According to REIWA's awards list for the prior financial year, Mr Li recorded $132 million worth of sales from 125 properties, netting him a prestigious top one per cent award.

This award was given to agents in Western Australia who sold the highest aggregate value of properties over the period, or the highest number.

Mr Li ranked 13th out of the 40 agents awarded the honour for the highest value of properties sold over the period.

When asked if he could guarantee that the data was reliable, given this year's discrepancies, Mr Li said he could not comment on how individual transactions may have affected the ranking.

"My priority is to ensure that the underlying sales information is accurate," he said.

REIWA president Suzanne Brown said the institute had been looking into Mr Li's sales data for around six months, prior to being contacted by the ABC.

REIWA president Suzanne Brown says the organisation audits the sales data provided by its member agents and takes its accuracy very seriously. (ABC News: Glynn Jones)

She said agents were responsible for providing accurate data, but the institute ran its own audits.

"We were already taking action and he has since been disqualified from obtaining an award this year," Ms Brown said.

She said the matter had been referred to REIWA's Professional Standards Tribunal.

"Depending on the recommendations and outcomes of this Tribunal will be whether the previous year's awards are removed from Roy Li," Ms Brown said.

"We really believe in the integrity of the awards and we do take them really seriously when we do find those inaccuracies," Ms Brown said.

title: Djokovic and Sabalenka stunned in US Open mixed doubles debut
text:
Top seeds Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka have suffered an early exit from the US Open mixed doubles, falling 1-4, 4-2, 10-2 to Henry Patten and Katerina Siniakova in their opening match.

Djokovic, a 24-time grand slam singles champion, and four-time major winner Sabalenka made a strong start by taking the opening set.

However, Patten and doubles specialist Siniakova hit back to claim the second before dominating the tiebreak to secure a place in the quarterfinals.

Siniakova sealed the upset in style with an ace out wide on match point, ending the tournament hopes of the star-studded pairing.

"It wasn't looking very good for a while," Patten said.

"In this format we play one bad game and all of a sudden the first set's gone.

"We knew the same could happen in the second, and we played an amazing tiebreak. Kat acing Novak on match point was great."

The mixed doubles championship is once again being staged in the week before the singles main draw, after organisers revamped the format last year to attract more leading singles players by reducing the field and giving the event a standalone slot on the calendar.

The revamped format proved a commercial success in its debut year, drawing sellout crowds and attracting many of the sport's biggest singles names despite criticism from some doubles specialists, who argued it marginalised established pairings.

Italian duo Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori went on to retain the title by defeating Iga Świątek and Casper Ruud in last year's final.

No problems for Williams and Alcaraz

Serena Williams (left) and Carlos Alcaraz (right) made a triumphant start to their US Open mixed doubles campaign. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Serena Williams made a triumphant return to the US Open, partnering with Carlos Alcaraz to beat Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool 5-3, 4-1 in the opening round.

The 23-time major winner had not competed at Arthur Ashe Stadium since her tearful farewell from the sport in 2022.

The crown jewel of American tennis erupted in deafening cheers as their queen took the court again.

The 44-year-old Williams had an easy rapport with Alcaraz, who is 21 years her junior, as the partners grinned and giggled their way into the quarterfinals, where they will meet Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli later on Tuesday.

"It's always such an amazing place to be here," Williams said. "I never expected to be back on this court."

Williams hit a backhand winner the first time she touched the ball, earning uproarious cheers from the packed house a little more than two months after she announced her stunning comeback.

After trading breaks, Williams blasted a 193.1kmh ace on the penultimate point in the seventh game, drawing audible gasps from the crowd. Alcaraz, who has not played since April due to injury, shook off the early rust to close out the set with a forehand winner.

They sprinted through the second set with ease, embracing after the win in their matching royal purple outfits.

"I'm playing next to the one and only Serena Williams," seven-times major winner Alcaraz said. "Trying to do the things she told me to do."

title: Root fuming as teammates 'continually keep making stupid mistakes'
text:
England captain Joe Root says he was "hacked off" and disappointed after another incident involving a teammate at a nightclub, adding that the national team players are trying to build a culture they can be proud of.

After videos on social media appeared to show England fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs being spoken to by police officers, England's Cricket Board (ECB) dropped the 31-year-old from the second test against Pakistan, which starts on Thursday.

Carse is the latest England cricketer to be involved in a nightclub incident after Harry Brook, Ben Duckett, former captain Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson, leading to accusations of a drinking culture amongst the players.

"If I'm being brutally honest, I'm really hacked off. I'm really disappointed," Root told reporters.

"It's not the isolated incident itself, it's the fact that we continually keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it's detracting from what we're doing on the field."

Root, who returned as England captain after Stokes retired from international cricket, said the players had taken the incidents seriously.

"Clearly, we're not portraying ourselves how we want to. I think we've got an opportunity to build a culture that's very strong, something we can be proud of. Of course that's not going to happen overnight," he added.

Brydon Carse is the latest England cricketer to be involved in an off-field incident. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley/Cricket Australia)

"We've already had conversations as a team about what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England, what it takes to play for England. They are very clear about what is expected of them, and how we need to go about things moving forward."

Root said he had spoken to Carse, who was replaced by Sonny Baker for the second Test.

"When I first found out, my first concern was him as a person … I don't think I'm speaking out of turn by saying he's very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I'm sure when he gets his chance, he'll say that himself," the captain added.

Carse was briefly arrested and no charges were brought. The independent Cricket Regulator will investigate whether he breached the ECB's code of conduct, the sport's national governing body said on Monday.

England, who won the first test by an innings and 103 runs, will next face Pakistan at Lord's, followed by a third test in Birmingham next month.

title: Axed by Abbott, backed by crowdfunders: How Amanda McKenzie keeps finding hope in a crisis
text:
From tech-platform shutdowns to defining national moments, the climate chief shares how public anger outpaced government policy – and how there is enormous power in telling better stories.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Amanda McKenzie – climate wunderkind, activist for hope and Climate Council chief executive – and her husband and two young children came down with COVID-19 recently, she got out the roller skates. She and her husband unearthed some jigsaw puzzles, turned their living room into a makeshift roller rink, and told the kids to have fun. Then, they went back to work in their home office. As she tells this story over lunch, I’m struck by two things. First, it says a lot about their commitment to community that McKenzie and her husband chose to lock down their family at home for a week, regardless of whether they were still symptomatic. And second: living in McKenzie’s house sounds like a hoot. We’re meeting at Patsy’s, a tranquil up-market vegetarian wine bar in Melbourne’s inner north, where almost all the produce prepared in the kitchen is grown in the owner’s regenerative farm in Victoria’s Central Highlands. McKenzie has nominated this lunch spot, which seems an almost too-perfect choice to interview one of the most senior women in Australia’s environment movement.

Advertisement

Zucchini flowers with almond crema and salsa al dragoncello at Patsy’s. Ruby Alexander “I’m quite a utilitarian eater, but my husband has a very bougie, foodie vibe, so he’s made me more of a foodie,” she says. “I think if I was just left to my own devices, I’d be just eating a salad … premixed leaves with sun-dried tomatoes or something.” Today, McKenzie eschews wine in favour of a pot of English breakfast tea, while I order a hibiscus spritz mocktail. It is a bougie wine bar, after all. McKenzie has lived almost half her life in the public eye, although she isn’t necessarily a household name outside environment circles. Her first leadership role came 20 years ago when, aged 23, she co-founded the Australian Youth Climate Coalition with fellow law graduate Anna Rose. The pair hit the ground running, growing a fledgling coalition of 27 youth groups to a national organisation numbering 100,000 members three years later. Anna Rose (left) and Amanda McKenzie pictured at their offices in Sydney in 2009. Peter Rae Back then, as she travelled around organising meetings and strategic campaigns, McKenzie often found herself the only woman in the room. There were many who underestimated this young woman and the importance of the message she was trying to convey.

Advertisement

“At that time, it was a ‘future issue’,” she says. “I talked about [the impacts on our] kids and grandchildren, and it strikes me now, these kids I was talking about 20 years ago, they’re here: they’re eight and five, and experiencing the impacts already.” Related Article Antarctica ‘It’s beginning to look a lot like the future’: Fears over sudden loss of sea ice Without intending to, it was former prime minister Tony Abbott who lit the fuse that propelled McKenzie into making her life’s mission the fight against climate change. In 2011, she joined the fledgling Australian Climate Commission as a senior communications adviser, determined to shift public debate on Australia’s changing climate. The commission was established by former prime minister Julia Gillard and led by Professor Tim Flannery. It was designed to provide independent advice on the science of climate change, and was announced as public alarm grew about climate change, fuelled by back-to-back La Nina weather events, and on the heels of the 1997-2010 millennium drought.

Advertisement

In its first report to government, The Critical Decade, commissioners warned that climate change “risks have never been clearer, and the case for action has never been more urgent”. Julia Gillard, then prime minister, received the first Australian Climate Commission report from chief Tim Flannery (left) and report author Will Steffen at Parliament House in 2011. Andrew Meares Less than two weeks after the Coalition came to power two years later, the commission’s time was up. In one of his first acts as environment minister, Greg Hunt phoned Flannery to tell him the commission would be axed, as part of the Abbott government’s commitment to scrap the carbon tax. “So very quietly, I’d just gone to the commissioners and said, ‘if we started a new thing, would you be up for it?’ And Tim Flannery was like, ‘Yes, let’s do it!’” After Hunt’s announcement, the commission issued a “relatively neutral response”, McKenzie says, stressing the importance of science to Australian democracy. Flannery held a press conference in which he praised Hunt’s “gracious” conduct in their conversation. Four days later, they officially launched The Climate Council, with founding commissioners including Flannery, the late Professor Will Steffen, Professor Veena Sahajwalla, Gerry Hueston and Professor Lesley Hughes.

Advertisement

“It just went crazy, as soon as it hit the media in the morning,” McKenzie says. “We did a bunch of radio, we started to do some TV news. Some of the newspapers had it. And then it started this big viral moment crowdfunding campaign. Professor Will Steffen addressing the media during a doorstop interview at Parliament House in Canberra in 2013. Alex Ellinghausen “Within that first day, we raised $500,000 and by the end of the day, Twitter [now X] thought we were buying followers, so they shut us down. PayPal thought we were money-laundering, so they shut us down because we’d raised money so fast ... It was this cyclone of activity.” They raised $1.3 million within the first week – more than the previous Climate Commission’s budget – from more than 15,000 people for whom Abbott’s cuts to climate commitments felt like attacks on science. Since then, the principle that “we should base our democratic debate on evidence”, as McKenzie puts it, has driven the way the Climate Council operates. Another element of the Climate Council’s approach is something akin to intentional hope.

title: The genius of Dolly Parton, the last great unifier in a divided nation
text:
Advertisement

CultureMusicVale Opinion The political genius of Dolly Parton, the great unifier Cory Alpert Former White House staffer August 26, 2026 — 11:39am

August 26, 2026 — 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The machinery of American politics sorts everything that it sees. Every moment becomes a litmus test, where every cultural symbol is judged as either MAGA or its opposite. Artists, companies, cities, sports, and even beer get assigned into these categories. A political age consumes everything it touches. Dolly Parton was one of the last major exceptions. Photo: Marija Ercegovac She managed a high-wire act of being entirely herself, a vision of American individualism done right, a preacher who could build a congregation without demanding conversion – where its members could briefly see a piece of shared humanity in each other in their shared appreciation of the woman we Americans knew as Saint Dolly.

Advertisement

Her first big break on the country music stage was as the “singing girl” on The Porter Wagoner Show. During her first performance, the audience booed her during the commercial break. They were angry at the change that this brash, blonde starlet with an unusual voice represented. Related Article Vale Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 The show allowed her star to rise, and eventually she set out on her own. Her break with Wagoner, then the kingmaker of country music, is what inspired Dolly to write I Will Always Love You. It’s a song about leaving someone you love but refusing to hate the person you’re leaving behind. The way that Dolly left Porter became the blueprint for a career as the last great unifier in American politics. Later in her life, when Porter was left poor at the end of his career, she bought his music catalogue and gifted it back to him. By the time she built her empire, she understood how fragile the kind of fame she had developed could be. In her flock were conservatives and liberals, evangelicals and atheists, drag queens and NASCAR drivers.

Advertisement

Gallery Gallery icon 7 images Vale Dolly Parton in Australia All the while, she refused to endorse anything while embracing everyone. Some of that instinct had been trained into her by country music’s famously possessive fans. When Dolly crossed into pop, she told TV talkshow host Larry King that she was worried that she was leaving those fans behind. But she told them that she wasn’t leaving country music. She was taking it with her. For many artists, that act would feel like cowardice, to never state your beliefs – to just shut up and sing. But Dolly Parton was anything but a coward. Instead, she was fearless about defining herself and refused to define anyone else.

Advertisement

In a 1984 interview with Andy Warhol, the painter told her that she could be a great preacher. She replied, “What do you mean? I am a great preacher.” Related Article Vale Dolly Parton wrote more than 3000 songs – but we’ve picked her top 10 What she preached was nothing short of American individualism done right. The internet today is flooded with her quotes and Dollyisms, using her very body to grant permission for her fans to become whatever ambitious, sequinned thing they are capable of becoming. Her only demand in return for that permission was to afford everyone else the same privilege. In the same interview, she talked about being a star, as finding your own place and shining within it. It does not require a big stage or a big wig. In Dolly’s universe, there was room enough for everyone to shine. Where I grew up in the rural South, imagination could often be hard to come by. Our school system was so underfunded that parts of it became known as the Corridor of Shame.

Advertisement

It’s the same world that Dolly grew up in. Her father couldn’t read, and the hard, patient life of the mountains of East Tennessee did not afford much possibility beyond those hills. Related Article Vale Beyond the wigs, there was always Dolly Parton’s wondrous wit and wisdom As Dolly’s star grew, she sent that possibility back. She sent books to every child in her home county until they were five years old. The program slowly expanded across the South, then across America. Last year, the Imagination Library delivered its 2 millionth book in Australia alone. Across the world, more than 300 million kids have gotten books – for many, it was the only way they would receive them. She was giving children the resources to decide who they might become. America often mistakes individualism for abandonment. The version that Dolly preached was that each of our lives belong to us, but she could give us each something that could make it larger.

Advertisement

Faith without works is dead, after all. The congregation of Dolly does not agree on every point. Dolly became the great unifier by creating a church big enough for everyone to find room for themselves. To love Dolly was to stand alongside people with whom you share little, and to understand that they have as much right to their place as you do. Dolly gave all of us a place where we could be different together. Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. title: Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyMiddle East at war Opinion Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard August 26, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump administration is hallucinating again. The United States’ “economic D-Day” against Iran will exhaust political consent in Washington for this ill-conceived war long before it forces Iran’s Revolutionary Guard to capitulate. It draws out the spectacle of Donald Trump’s aimless flailing in a region that neither he nor his close advisers begin to understand, further convulsing the global energy, food and commodity markets and further eviscerating US strategic credibility. Even if Trump turns the dial up to 11, he may not get the response that he wants. AP The plan to mount the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary” requires also mobilising China, Russia, India, Turkey, a resentful Europe and the world’s major financial centres in a joint campaign to throttle Iran, a country that has already learned to live with 2200 separate US sanctions. The US Treasury could plausibly have pulled off such a feat 10 to 15 years ago, when it was able to crush nations by the “boa constrictor” method, using all the tools of the world’s dollarised financial system. But that supremacy relied on a tight-knit phalanx of democratic allies – or what we used to call the West. Such a world no longer exists, and China cannot be pushed around any longer.

Advertisement

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened the economic obliteration of any country that declines to enlist as foot soldiers in America’s quarrel. “If you insist on doing business with them – either transferring money, buying their oil, doing seaborne ship transport – the US government will put its full might and force toward enforcing against you,” he said. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war The White House says this is the Iran endgame. We’ve heard that before Such hubris is courting fate for a nation that depends on constant inflows of capital from these same countries to fund its twin deficits and that already has to pay punitive interest rates to sell its bonds. The US Treasury made a Faustian pact by issuing so much short-term debt. The trap is closing. Bessent must roll over or fund almost $US6 trillion ($8.4 trillion) every three months in a hostile market. The budget deficit was $US432 billion for the single month of July, up 48 per cent from the year before.

Advertisement

Trump has a solution for this and a warning for any bond investor who declines to feed his appetite. “We have many types of intervention. The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will,” he said. Does he intend to parachute the 101st Airborne into London’s Canary Wharf and Singapore’s harbour district to cart off pension fund managers in shackles for interrogation at Guantanamo? The move draws out the spectacle of Donald Trump’s aimless flailing in a region that neither he nor his close advisers begin to understand, further convulsing the global energy, food and commodity markets. AP It is normal to dial up pressure by starting with economic sanctions before escalating to killing people. Everybody can see that Trump is doing it the other way round because killing has comprehensively failed. The world can see that the US is overstretched, lacks sufficient military power to enforce its will, has exhausted two-thirds of its Patriot interceptors and “virtually all” its surface-to-surface (ATACMS) missiles, and has denuded its defences in the Far East. It can see that the US lacks the stomach for a full ground invasion of Iran and anything short of that is whistling in the wind.

Advertisement

Iran can see all of this too. The regime has survived a bombing campaign and the assassination of 180 members of its leadership. Sanctions are almost laughable at this juncture. Related Article Middle East at war US military top brass dispatched to aircraft carrier rocked by talk of crumbling morale Iran’s land border stretches for 5900 kilometres across seven countries, most of them either friendly or cynically transactional. The frontier rises in an arc from Pakistan to the Eurasian heartland around the Caspian Sea, then down the other side to Turkey and the entire eastern side of Iraq. It is impossible to sustain a goods blockade. The International North-South Transport Corridor already runs as a rail freight link from Russia through Central Asia to Iran. The maritime route via the Caspian does a booming trade as well. Russia cannot export much grain through the Black Sea right now because of Ukrainian drones, so it is exporting what it can to Iran and through Iranian proxies to the wider Middle East. Ergo, a) Iran will have enough food for itself even if its economy is in dire straits and b) Iran will gain strategic leverage as a grain conduit to a region facing serious food stress.

Advertisement

China currently buys 90 per cent of Iran’s oil and in return China sells it machinery, vehicles and electronics, including sensors and engines for Iran’s Shahed drones as well as propellants for its ballistic missiles. China will not let the US dictate how and with whom it may trade. It has gone to some lengths to demonstrate this objection. The world knows that an overstretched America lacks the capability and stomach for a full invasion of Iran. Getty Images If Washington imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese banks and entities, Beijing has a rich menu of retaliation, starting with curbs on critical minerals. Bessent has demonstrated by his actions that he fears rising US bond yields. Beijing knows this, and if it wants to rattle his cage, it can play a few hedge fund tricks of its own by weaponising $US4 trillion of dollar assets held by the Chinese central bank, the state-controlled commercial banks and the giant state-policy banks.

Advertisement

If the US does impose secondary sanctions on Chinese banks, it will have to do the same to European banks that do business with China, otherwise the financial blockade breaks down. But the European Union now has its blocking statute aimed at forbidding its own companies from complying with US extraterritorial sanctions or submitting to US coercion. Iran has a say in the matter too and may choose to hold Trump’s feet to the fire, exploiting the window between now and the midterm elections to cause commodity havoc while always staying just below the threshold of total conflagration. It is normal to dial up pressure by starting with economic sanctions before escalating to killing people. Everybody can see that Trump is doing it the other way round because killing has comprehensively failed. “If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf,” said Mohsen Rezaee, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. That too is bluster, but it is closer to the truth than the US cares to admit. Iran still controls the Strait of Hormuz and has a second partial stranglehold over the Red Sea via its Houthi allies.

Advertisement

It still has a sufficient arsenal of drones and missiles hidden in mountains to strike commercial shipping at will and enough to inflict serious damage to the energy infrastructure of the Gulf states. The rest of us are condemned to months of mounting stress in the global hydrocarbon markets as storage falls to critically low levels and even greater stress in the markets for diesel, petrol and jet fuel. Despite Trump’s assertions, Iran still controls the Strait of Hormuz. Getty Images The refined petroleum products that we consume are trading today at levels equivalent to crude oil prices of $US140 to $US160 a barrel. The IATA jet fuel index is $US170 in Europe and $US165 in the US.

Advertisement

Wholesale diesel costs $US185 in New York harbour and $US180 in Rotterdam, and it is diesel that fuels farming, trucking, construction and swaths of the industrial economy on both sides of the Atlantic. Natural gas prices in Europe are trading this week at €69 ($112) per megawatt-hour, higher than the panic peak at the onset of Trump’s Iran war. European inventories are disturbingly low for this time of the year, and Britain has almost no safety buffer. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will face his first big crisis if this northern winter proves harsh. These commodity costs are becoming embedded in the global supply chain, are already visible in rising bond yields and will soon be visible in rising inflation and the cost of living. It is hard to see any way out of this impasse, since Trump has only two options: either to accept defeat on Iranian terms, which become more exigent by the week, or to mobilise the US for a long, bloody and costly war that consumes his presidency and may also end in defeat. He shrinks from both.

Manhattan Gold Corporation has delivered another round of strong, broad gold intercepts from its Jaws prospect in Nunavut, Canada, with drilling extending the known mineralised system by more than 150 metres to the southwest. The latest results from the company’s maiden drill campaign at its Hook Lake project include a significant 25.9-metre hit grading 1.59 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 89.92m, which housed a richer 6.1-metre core at 3.62g/t gold. Manhattan Gold’s Hook Lake project area in Nunavut, Canada. Other notable intersections from this second batch of assays included 35.05m at 1.23g/t gold from 124.97m, with a 9.14-metre slice of 2.52g/t, and 22.86m at 2.37g/t gold from a shallower 74.68m. The latter intercept contained a particularly spicy 1.52-metre section grading a hefty 26.8g/t gold. The results land at a time when Canada’s vast northern territory of Nunavut is proving to be a hot address for gold explorers. Home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast and one of Canada’s largest gold mines, peers such as B2Gold and Fury Gold Mines are also advancing programs, underlining the district-scale appetite for new ounces. With the gold price recently pushing higher to more than US$4600 (A$6400) per ounce, any exploration success is getting a serious second look from the market.

Advertisement

‘The Jaws system remains open along strike and at depth.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard Manhattan says the latest intercepts from its Jaws target are returning thicker, higher-grade results than those recorded in nearby historic drilling from 1988, suggesting the company’s modern exploration approach is already paying dividends and adding material upside to the historical data. Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard said:“Drilling at Jaws continues to deliver multiple broad gold zones with higher grade internal cores, led by 25.90 metres at 1.59g/t gold. Drill results including JWS26005 and JWS26006, also highlight the material upside compared to historic drilling by revealing thicker and higher-grade intercepts when compared to the nearest 1988 drillholes.” Jaws, the most advanced target at Hook Lake, hosts a non-JORC foreign estimate of 3.4 million tonnes at 2.38g/t gold for 285,000 ounces of gold, defined by drilling in the late 1980’s. Manhattan’s current program has been designed to confirm and potentially expand on that historic work. Notably, the company’s work has also recalibrated the geological map. Manhattan says its new drilling has shifted the interpreted position of the gold-bearing main shear zone 20m to 30m northwest of where historic records had placed it, providing the company with a sharper geological model for follow-up drilling. The revised geometry of the orebody provides a much stronger basis for follow-up drill targeting and may open up previously under-explored zones.

With the rods still turning at Jaws, Manhattan is looking at a bigger picture for the deposit. The company has assays pending for a further 12 drillholes, including a key hole that tested below the footprint of all historic drilling at Jaws, opening up the possibility for new mineralisation lurking below. The pending results also include the first-ever drill tests of the company’s Spectre and Lotus prospects. Spectre is a high-grade volcanogenic massive sulphide target where historic drilling in 1974 returned impressive polymetallic hits including 10.51 metres at 2.91 per cent copper, 6.70 per cent zinc, 95.67g/t silver and 1.04g/t gold. The Lotus prospect, described as a “Jaws-style” gold target, has never been drilled despite rock chip sampling in 2025 returning high-grade results of 8.01g/t gold and 2660g/t silver. With drilling at Jaws continuing to deliver broad zones of gold, a historic resource to build upon and a pipeline of assays from both extension and new discovery targets, Manhattan doesn’t look short of catalysts. As the company continues to piece together the puzzle at Hook Lake, punters will likely be watching closely for what the drill bit uncovers next.
