Exclusive NationalNSWArchitecture A loo with a view and no railings on ‘an impossible site’ in Sydney Julie Power August 26, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Holland House in Sydney’s Middle Cove was as famous for its architecture as it was for a ballet performed on the cantilevered terrace that hovers 12 metres above rock and bush. The balcony had no handrails. The cliff top home on an impossible site at 31 Rembrandt Drive was designed by one of Sydney’s most divisive architects, Neville Gruzman, and is now on the market for the first time in 40 years and with balustrades for safety. “Gruzman was a Sydney sensualist,” said Tone Wheeler, who was among the first of dozens of architects to visit the first open house. He was referring to Holland House’s changing floor levels, its rich materials and the sunken lounge near a copper fireplace.

Advertisement

Holland House, 31 Rembrandt Drive, Middle Cove Domain Inspired by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright and Japanese architecture, Gruzman was known for over-the-top mid-century homes. He catered to clients like the Hollands who liked to entertain, and weren’t afraid of the cost or making a big statement. (Having confidence to sit on a toilet in front of a wall of glass helped, too.) Holland House, c 1962, by Sydney architect and former Woollahra mayor Neville Gruzman is on the market. Julie Power At 165 square metres, the three-bedroom home now being marketed by The Agency is about 100 square metres smaller than most new builds.

Advertisement

The house, set on an 859-square-metre block, is not heritage listed, though it is included with other homes by Gruzman on Docomomo Australia Modern Register. Gruzman, the mayor of Woollahra in 1996, was known for being litigious, initiating 30 cases in 40 years. After his death, fellow architects described him as a stirrer, and a man who made loyal friends and mortal enemies. Like the Sydney homes he designed, he was complex, unusual, and difficult to categorise. Reviewing the Hollands new home in 1967 for Australian Home Journal, architect Basil Beirman wrote that its success on one of the most difficult sites he had seen gave his “jaded architectural palate a stimulating lift”. Beirman loved everything, except the lack of railings. They “might be acceptable at three or four feet [a metre] above the ground, but [at] 30 or 40 feet was not.” “Hand-rails might spoil the terraces aesthetically, and balustrades spoil the view. But if the owners share, even a little, my dislike of standing so high without any apparent safeguard, I don’t think it will be long before they do something about it,” he wrote.

Advertisement

Wheeler said Gruzman would take an idea and then push it to excess. Holland House’s design was “dramatic and relentless with the entire eastern wall covered in windows.” Gruzman designed a dressing room for his wife Margot at their Darling Point home that was wall-to-wall mirrors. The dressing room that architect Neville Gruzman designed for his wife had mirrors everywhere. Louise Kennerley The late architect Bruce Rickard, said every Gruzman design was different yet had several elements in common. “They have a beautiful spatial flow, the living areas all face north, and they are exquisitely detailed.” Gruzman thought he was Sydney’s best architect, bar none, said Wheeler. He was also quick to criticise others, including Harry Seidler – considered one of Australia’s greatest – and launched a personal attack on Wheeler at one stage.

Advertisement

He famously liked to compare himself with Wright, and was proud that Opera House designer Jørn Utzon had said the living room in his family home was the best in all of Australia. To his fans, Gruzman was one of Sydney’s most innovative post-war architects. A book on great Sydney homes said Holland House was built on “an impossible site” so steep that it was virtually a cliff. Its wraparound windows created the impression of a fully transparent Japanese screen. At night, it was transformed into a glowing lantern. The view from the toilet and bath is spectacular, said Julie Power, pictured, but the view of the bathroom from the deck outside is probably less attractive. Nicky Catley Look no handrail. In a file photo, the terrace seems to float about 10 metres above the bush next to sheer cliff. The former Gruzman family home at Oswald Street, Darling Point.

title: This town has finally realised its potential as the perfect beach getaway
text:
Advertisement

InspirationQueensland This town has finally realised its potential as the perfect beach getaway Julietta Jameson Updated August 26, 2026 — 11:27am ,first published August 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This article is part of our comprehensive guide to the Sunshine Coast, your guide to where to stay, eat and the must-see highlights. See all stories .

Common wisdom says galleries and museums are the mark of a fully formed destination. I believe it’s coffee. At least this is the conclusion I reach over a latte at Cici’s Continental Deli, a hole-in-the-wall cafe a stone’s throw from Mooloolaba Beach. It’s a cave-like refuge from all that Sunshine Coast sunshine (though of course there’s outdoor seating), with clever mid-century styling that makes it feel decades older than 2025 when it opened. The coffee is excellent, the sandwiches generous and the attitude distinctly Sunshine Coast: friendly, relaxed and chatty. Mooloolaba Beach, on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast, has come of age. The last time I was here, more than a decade ago, finding decent coffee required local knowledge. Friends who lived there pointed me in the right direction. This time I simply stumble across it. If not fully formed in the way top destinations are, Mooloolaba, I think, is at least growing up. Could it be the new Noosa, the aspirational jewel in the Sunshine Coast crown? Queensland coastal destinations have never needed museums for holiday crowds to think of them as the perfect getaway. What they need is sun, sand, surf and lifestyle.

Advertisement

Despite having all that, Mooloolaba has had the reputation for being a bit, well, daggy. Locals and regular holidaymakers have liked it that way. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. But there’s change in the air and on the ground, and it’s the kind that can turn daggy to de rigueur. Mooloolaba prawns fresh from the trawler at Mooloolaba Marina. Of course, with its ’80s architecture along the main drag, a population of retirees who favour trackie dacks over palazzo pants, and a cohort of triathlete types who prefer Lycra to linen, Mooloolaba is a fair way from today’s Noosa, where high-end shopping, celebrity chefs and luxury holidays are part of the brand. But if we’re talking about the Noosa people remember fondly – the one a Facebook group is devoted to under the moniker “I remember Noosa before it was cool” – then Mooloolaba is surely a contender.

Advertisement

It’s a leap to declare all this on the back of finding a great cafe. In fact, it’s almost contradictory. Good coffee can be a gateway drug to parking problems and other conditions that make a place insufferable. The Mooloolaba Spit separates the Pacific Ocean from the Mooloolah River. But for now, Mooloolaba is having a moment, balancing lived character with contemporary sophistication – and that’s in no small part due to the new Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel, the first full-service internationally branded new-build hotel on the Sunshine Coast in four decades. With a young, enthusiastic staff, there’s a real sense of place at the Avani. It’s a $50 million landmark development that runs to the seaside-holiday playbook perfectly. It’s got beachy tones in a relaxed decor that pops with decorative accents and an airy sense of space. Rooms have balconies, many of which have big ocean views and beds oriented for a sunrise wake-up. The story of the site on which it sits is emblematic of the town’s change. Just a block back from the beach, hence premium real estate, it was previously an expansive council-owned ground-level carpark. Council sold off half – that became the hotel – while the other half was developed into a far more efficient multilevel parking structure.

Advertisement

Avani Mooloolaba’s highlight is its upper reaches. There’s a rooftop infinity pool and terrace, and Sully’s Rooftop, the hotel’s signature restaurant, eagerly patronised by locals. Later this year at street level, First Avenue Cellar & Bar will also open, joining the excellent Lobby Bar (another spot for good coffee). The Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel is the first new full-service hotel to hit the Sunshine Coast in 40 years. A bedroom with an uninterruped beach view inside the Avani hotel in Mooloolaba. The 180 rooms span 12 storeys in line with local height restrictions, meaning no Gold Coast-style shadows on the beach. Mooloolaba’s second luxury hotel, though, the Aria development just down the road, will be bigger, with council recently approving two extra storeys on the basis of needing additional hotel rooms in the region.

Advertisement

Locals worry about such incremental height creep. Up to now, though, their biggest worry amid all the change, has been the demolition of Mooloolaba’s much-loved but undeniably dated “loo with a view”, a badly placed public convenience that blocked the beach view and became a joke’s punchline. It makes way for a foreshore precinct that is currently under construction and which features boardwalks, terraced sea walls and community facilities Seafood eatery Prawn Star inhabits a couple of converted prawn trawlers and a pontoon. Those same priorities have seen Mooloolaba Wharf become a lively hub of hospitality. Too often, old wharf precincts can become Disneyfied white elephants. But here, the wharf is still in regular use for boating purposes, and the boutiques, cafes and eateries are packed with visitors and locals alike. A highlight is Prawn Star, a seafood-serving institution inhabiting a couple of converted prawn trawlers and a pontoon. A didgeridoo performance during a Salwater Eco Tours cruise. One morning, we leave the wharf with Simon Thornalley, founder of Indigenous tourism operator, Saltwater Eco Tours, for a cruise on Gubbi Gubbi/Kabi Kabi Country. His boat is a 1908 heritage-listed sailing vessel that he restored himself. It’s big on character and is a good match for Thornalley’s.

Advertisement

The Mooloolah River has an extensive canal network and cruising on it, we pass mansions, including one owned by the Irwins with their research boat parked out the front. Most of our admiration is for the remaining little 1960s and ’70s holiday shacks. The juxtaposition makes me reflect on what we lose to the same progress I admire. The losses to Thornalley’s people, however, are on a far greater scale and on a much longer timeline. He doesn’t dwell on it. Instead, as we munch on a morning tea, he points out birds and land forms, tells stories of the water, and as our cruise nears its end, he treats us to a didgeridoo performance. Paddling out with Saltwater Eco Tours. On a sunset cruise with Set Sail Cruises, it’s all about simply admiring the coast from both the river and the ocean. We crank up a yacht-rock playlist, pop the bubbly, and enjoy the wind in our hair and spray on our faces. In Mooloolaba there are whale watching cruises, snorkelling and diving cruises, turtle activities, canoeing, paddleboarding and kayaking adventures, and so much more. The fact it’s so jam-packed with activities is what makes it fundamentally different to Noosa, a local tells me. “Noosa’s about being seen, we’re about doing.”

Advertisement

At Sea Life Sunshine Coast it’s hard to argue. It’s a favourite with families but behind the penguins, seals and underwater tunnel is one of the region’s most important marine rescue operations, rehabilitating injured turtles before returning them to the ocean. It’s a reminder that, for all its growing sophistication, Mooloolaba remains closely connected to the marine environment that built it. You can admire the coast from both the river and the ocean on a boat trip with Set Sail Cruises. Then there’s the Lycra brigade. The Mooloolaba Triathlon is Australia’s second-largest triathlon event. Held annually in mid-March, the festival attracts about 9000 competitors across elite and amateur categories, with the ocean swims, sprint and cycling standard Olympic distances. For those looking to recover from all that, even wellness has become part of the town’s evolution. Once upon a time, a surf followed by fish and chips probably qualified as self-care here, and it probably still does to many. Today, visitors can alternate beach walks with infrared saunas, ice baths, massage treatments and spa rituals. Tank Bathhouse has helped introduce communal bathing culture to the Sunshine Coast, while Sauna & Ice Studio caters to the growing enthusiasm for hot-and-cold therapy. The Avani has also introduced a terrific spa to the equation. Not only are the treatments top tier, but the hotel, which runs the spa itself, has priced products competitively (rather than at the enormous mark-ups many hotel spas favour), making it a lovely retail experience as well as a healing one.

Advertisement

Amid the touristy restaurants with touts out the front, the ice-cream vendors and dark entryways to the plethora of short-term apartment accommodation that is the lifeblood of Mooloolaba stays, the esplanade is home to some terrific boutiques. The Wharf Mooloolaba has gelato, sushi, tacos, a bakery and plenty of atmosphere. A standout is Zambezee, where international women’s fashion brands hang next to quality local designers. Avenue J deals in exquisitely curated antique jewellery and some lovely objets d’art. Even the pharmacy has some great finds in the form of Queensland-made cosmetics, candles and hair accessories. It’s not Noosa-level retail therapy, but that pharmacy is perhaps one of the best illustrations of the Mooloolaba change: it’s locally focused with a side of sophistication, rather than sophistication first, local second. Sure, there is increasing style here: better coffee, better restaurants and better places to stay. There will be more thoughtful public spaces. But it feels like the natural evolution of a beach town that is realising its potential, while still maintaining its own unique character. And in that, there’s no need for it to be “the new” anywhere, other than the destination it is.

title: Dolly Parton wrote more than 3000 songs – but we’ve picked her top 10
text:
Starting as a country singer in the early 1960s before crossing into pop at the end of the 70s, Parton has an enduring musical legacy. These are her top hits.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From her origins as a country singer in the early 1960s before crossing over into pop and bluegrass genres at the end of the ’70s, Dolly Parton, who died overnight on Wednesday (AEST) aged 80, has an enduring musical legacy. Even today’s superstars, including Beyoncé, Sabrina Carpenter and goddaughter Miley Cyrus, gush about the honour of duetting with Parton. I may have been born decades after the pinnacle of Parton’s musical reign, but she remains one of the few artists who cut through my generation (those born post 9/11). Her track 9 to 5 inspired me to unionise at McDonald’s as a teenage fry cook – and many girls in high school to play percussion with their acrylic nails. Parton wrote her first song when she was six years old, the simple story of “Little Tiny Tasseltop” based on a doll her mother made from a corncob. Over her career she composed more than 3000 songs – making it no easy task to rank her top 10. Tell us what your favourite Dolly songs are in the comments below. 10. Two Doors Down (1977) This heartwarming country melody about a woman who goes to a party just down the hall – or two doors down – to get over a particularly melancholic breakup was released on Parton’s 1977 album Here You Come Again.

Advertisement

She ends up bringing back a “new love” to her place, which, conveniently, is only two doors down! Parton puts the saying that to get over someone you should get under someone, to a country-pop bop. 9. Here You Come Again (1977) The song that earned Parton her first Grammy for Best Female Country Vocal Performance and namesake of her 19th studio album, Here You Come Again, went on to be her first million-selling record. About feeling as though she’s finally over a man until she looks into his eyes and sees his smile, the country-pop song was one of Parton’s most popular when she began mixing country and pop genres. 8. Do I Ever Cross Your Mind, with Chet Atkins (1982)

Advertisement

A bittersweet country-pop melody about a lingering love – and wondering if your ex still thinks about you – fills you with a sense of nostalgia. Parton’s giggles and the playful back-and-forth with guitarist Atkins makes the tune so tender. “I love you,” she says at the end. Released on her 1982 album Heartbreak Express alongside another hit, I Will Always Love You. 7. My Tennessee Mountain Home (1973) Country-folk at Parton’s finest, the song is a tribute to her childhood being raised in the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee. Honeysuckles, June bugs, front porches, eagles, Sunday mass and crickets singing in nearby fields. A song made during her country era, it’s warm and fuzzy. “Life is as peaceful as a baby’s sigh,” Parton sings. 6. Light of a Clear Blue Morning (1977)

Advertisement

Whenever you feel down, and you’ve got the blues, there is a guaranteed Parton song to lift your spirits and give you an aural pat on the back. This ballad turned upbeat pop track was the opening song on her New Harvest ... First Gathering album. According to Rolling Stone, Parton refers to this hit as “my song of deliverance” after walking out of her former professional partner Porter Wagoner’s office and driving home in a storm before the sky opened, shining golden rays on her. 5. Islands in the Stream, with Kenny Rogers (1982) Now we’re entering the territory of Parton’s biggest hits. Named Country Music Television’s number one country duet of all time in 2005, the enchanting classic originally composed by the Bee Gees brought together two solo artists at the peak of their careers. According to Rolling Stone, the hit has sold more than two million copies in the US. 4. 9 to 5 (1980) The song that brought me to discover Parton’s discography – and workers’ rights. It opens with one of the most classic intros known to girl-kind, the clinking of acrylic nails. The iconic beat (dare I say more than Queen’s We Will Rock You) was fashioned when Parton did not have her guitar handy and began rubbing her nails together to mimic a typewriter. It was recorded for the 1980 comedy 9 to 5. With nearly 900 million streams on Spotify, the track went on to win two Grammys for Parton and dominated the US charts.

Advertisement

3. I Will Always Love You (1974) The song the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll, Elvis Presley, wanted to record so badly he was willing to buy the copyright – or even settle for half. Unlucky for him, no amount could purchase it from Parton. “I wouldn’t let Colonel Tom Parker [record the song],” Parton said when asked about the then-rumour in a 2023 interview on BBC 2 Radio. “Because Elvis loved the song. In fact, I talked to Priscilla not very long ago; she said, ‘You know, Elvis sang that song to me when we were walking down the courthouse steps when we got divorced’.” Related Article Vale Beyond the wigs, there was always Dolly Parton’s wondrous wit and wisdom “The night before [the recording session], Colonel Tom Parker calls me and says, ‘Well, you know we don’t record anything with Elvis unless we have publishing on it, or at least half the publishing,’ … Well, I said because I had a number one song on it, I said, ‘This is the most important copyright in my whole publishing company, and I can’t do that.’ “And I just didn’t do it, and they just didn’t do it. But I always wondered what it would sound like. I know he’d kill it. Don’t you? He would have killed it. But anyway, so he didn’t. Then when Whitney [Houston’s version] came out, I made enough money to buy Graceland.”

title: The Queen of Country: Dolly Parton's life in pictures
text:
Dolly Parton, the country music star who rose from grinding poverty in Tennessee to become a rhinestone-studded cultural icon with hits like Jolene and 9 to 5, has died at 80, her family said on Wednesday.

Dolly Parton performing in 1974. Source: Getty / Michael Ochs Archives

Dolly Parton with Johnny Cash (left) and Ronnie Milsap. Hosting a show at Nashville's Grand Ole Opry, Cash introduced a 13-year-old Parton as "a little girl here from up in East Tennessee". Source: Getty / Bettmann Archive

Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on 19 January 1946 in Sevierville, Tennessee, the fourth of 12 children who grew up dirt-poor in the family's small shack in the Great Smoky Mountains.

Parton's work with collaborator and co-producer Porter Wagoner transformed her sound, launching her career. Source: Getty / Michael Ochs Archives

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

With time, Parton's relationship with Wagoner would fray, ending in a 1979 legal battle over royalties. Source: Getty / Michael Ochs Archives

Parton was more than a singer — she wrote 3,000 songs, acted in major Hollywood films and donated millions of dollars to charities in her home state and beyond.

Dolly Parton and her rarely-seen, long-time partner, Carl Dean. They married in the mid 1960s and were together until his death at 82 in 2025. Source: Getty / Vinnie Zuffante

Dolly Parton's stage persona — of a sparkling, peroxide blonde bombshell — was carefully crafted by Parton herself as part of a wildly successful business strategy. Source: Getty / Richard E Aaron

She was also an accomplished businesswoman, with her interests spanning from her popular Dollywood theme park to cosmetics, pet apparel, baking mixes and even a truck stop.

Dolly Parton maintained a roster of voluminous wigs and rhinestone-covered jumpsuits. Source: Getty / David Redfern

As a performer, Dolly Parton was a mixture of Southern charm, humour and glamour. But fans also considered her a feminist role model for holding the reins of her own career in an entertainment world dominated by men. Source: Getty / Richard McCaffrey

During a prolific career that spanned six decades, Parton penned hits such as Jolene, Coat of Many Colours and the iconic ballad I Will Always Love You, which became an international success for Whitney Houston.

Parton famously wrote two of her most famous country standards, Jolene and I Will Always Love You, on the same day. Source: Getty / Richard E Aaron

By the late 1970s, Parton had transitioned to a more pop music sound, a contentious move at the time. Source: Getty / Paul Natkin

Never one to downplay her striking looks, Parton essentially wrote the book on how a woman can rule the airwaves in a male-dominated industry, with songs covered by everyone from Shania Twain to Sinead O'Connor.

Parton recorded arguably her most famous duet, Islands in the Stream, with Kenny Rogers in 1983. Source: AAP / AP / Doug Pizac

Dolly Parton's friendship with Kenny Rogers would last until his death in 2020. Source: Getty / Rick Diamond

The US singer-songwriter, actress, businesswoman and philanthropist didn't seem to mind being mistaken for a ditzy blonde all too eager to play up her looks, after growing up poor in rural Tennessee.

Parton was godmother to singer Miley Cyrus. The pair performed Jolene at the 61st annual Grammy Awards in 2019. Source: AAP / AP / Matt Sayles

Dolly Parton launched the Imagination Library, a children's literacy scheme, as part of her Dollywood theme park in Tennessee. Source: AAP / Rui Vieira

At the height of her fame, she reached number one on the pop charts, with songs like Islands in the Stream, and starred in Hollywood blockbusters 9 to 5, for which she sang the insuppressible title track, and Steel Magnolias.

Dolly Parton's Dollywood theme park (seen here in 1993) is still a major economic driver for the Southern Appalachian region. Source: Getty / Ron Davis

Dolly Parton ran the bulk of her business operations from her office in Nashville, a site which was also used for the occasional photoshoot. Source: AAP / AP / John Russell

She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022.

Parton initially turned down the honour, saying she felt she hadn't earned it. She released a rock album, Rockstar, in 2023, which she called an attempt to justify the induction.

Dolly Parton was one of the most decorated musicians of all time, and a regular nominee at music awards shows across her long career. Source: AAP / AP / Matt Sayles

Dolly Parton was an extraordinarily prolific artist. In her career, she produced 49 studio albums, four collaborative albums, nine live albums, six soundtrack albums, one extended play and approximately 222 compilation albums globally. Source: Getty / NBCUniversal

Affording her the sort of honour given to major state figures, US President Donald Trump ordered flags across the country to be lowered for a week to mark what he called a "true loss for millions of people".

Fans have mourned Dolly Parton's passing near her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Source: AAP / EPA / Chris Torres

— With Agence France-Presse.

title: Australia's runway warning: What 22 years of data reveal
text:
In brief Close calls at Sydney Airport have put air traffic control safety under the microscope.

Data analysis reveals the many moving parts that contribute to runway incursions.

Four close calls on Sydney Airport runways in as many weeks have put air traffic management in the spotlight.

It’s too early to determine the exact cause of each one. But four ground-safety occurrences at Australia’s busiest airport in a little over three weeks raise an obvious question: how common are occurrences like these, and are they becoming more frequent?

To examine the broader pattern, I analysed Australian Transport Safety Bureau data from 2003 to 2025 for Australian commercial air transport, focusing on runway incursions (the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person in a protected runway area) and taxiing collisions or near collisions (an aircraft colliding or nearly colliding with another aircraft, person or object while taxiing).

What happened at Sydney Airport?

The most recent incident occurred just after 8am last Tuesday, when two planes were given permission to use the same runway at the same time. Luckily, one plane stopped when its pilot saw the other plane.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

A little over a week earlier, on August 9, there were two more incidents in less than three hours.

At 7.20am, a Jetstar Airbus A320 preparing to depart for the Gold Coast encountered an empty Qatar Airways Boeing 777 being towed across a taxiway. Both planes stopped abruptly. One Jetstar cabin crew member sustained a serious injury.

Then, at about 10am, a Virgin Australia Boeing 737 bound for Perth began its take-off sequence on a runway as a Qantas 737 crossed another runway ahead. Both crews reported having received the relevant clearance from air traffic control. The Virgin crew stopped as air traffic control cancelled its take-off clearance.

On July 27, air traffic control cleared a Qantas Boeing 737 to cross a runway while a smaller plane was still landing. Air traffic control detected the issue and alerted both crews, with the 737 stopping after passing the holding point.

Near-collisions have increased significantly

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau investigates and reports on safety incidents involving planes, helicopters, trains and boats. These incidents include those that happen during taxiing, takeoff and landing.

Raw counts of reported occurrences can be misleading because aviation activity has varied substantially, particularly during the COVID pandemic. More flying creates more risk. So I also calculated occurrence rates per million flight hours, for both domestic aviation and all commercial air transport, which includes domestic aviation as well as other forms of aviation such as freight and charter.

For domestic aviation, analysis of the annual data from 2003 to 2025 shows a significant increasing underlying trend in both the number and rate of taxiing collisions or near-collisions. Across the period, the number increased on average by about one additional occurrence every three years. The significant increase in the rate indicates this trend cannot simply be explained by growth in aviation activity.

Across all commercial air transport, taxiing collisions or near-collisions have also increased significantly in number, but not in rate. This suggests increased aviation activity explains at least part of the rise.

Runway incursions show the clearest commercial air transport trend, with significant increases in both their number and rate per million flight hours. Across the period, the number increased on average by about three additional runway incursions every two years.

Neither the count nor rate of <strong>domestic runway incursions has increased significantly.

The distinction between number and rate matters. Increasing occurrence counts can reflect greater aviation activity, while an increasing rate indicates the number of occurrences are rising faster than the amount of flying.

Frequency is only half the picture

Aviation safety occurrences are classified as:

accidents (where serious injury/death or substantial aircraft damage/destruction actually occurred).

serious incidents (where an accident was narrowly avoided)

incidents (all other occurrence, which affects or could affect the safety of operation)

This reflects both their consequences and how close they came to a substantially worse outcome.

The four recent Sydney occurrences illustrate this. The July runway incursion and Jetstar/Qatar taxiing near-collision are classified as serious incidents, while the Virgin/Qantas runway incursion is classified as an incident.

The fourth occurrence has not yet appeared in the Australian Transport Safety Bureau’s database. But the bureau has indicated it will also be classified as an incident because there was no immediate risk of collision.

The most striking result from the data is for domestic taxiing collisions and near-collisions. While accidents account for only 0.05 per cent of all domestic aviation events, they account for 2.16 per cent of taxiing events. Three of the 29 domestic aviation accidents recorded since 2003 were taxiing collisions. That’s more than one in ten.

Runway incursions have in general been much less serious. Almost 98 per cent were classified as incidents, with accidents absent from the domestic data and accounting for only 0.10 per cent of commercial air transport runway incursions.

But although most runway incursions are classified as incidents, they can create the conditions for a collision if other safety barriers fail.

Should passengers be concerned?

Four occurrences at one airport in less than a month understandably attract attention. But a cluster does not by itself demonstrate that Sydney Airport has suddenly become unsafe.

The occurrences were operationally different, and the Australian Transport Safety Bureau investigations will determine how each developed and why the available safety barriers did not prevent the conflicts from arising.

Some have suggested air traffic control staffing pressures may be relevant. For example, Civil Air president Scott Nugent said there are not enough air traffic controllers in Australia, that Sydney Airport has relied heavily on overtime, and that some controllers may be working more than 20 additional hours a week.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau will also examine whether understaffing at Sydney Airport played any role in the recent occurrences.

Whatever the investigations ultimately find about the causes of these recent occurrences, the historical data answer a broader question. What matters is not whether more occurrences are being reported, but whether they are becoming more frequent relative to aviation activity and whether their severity is changing.

For runway incursions involving commercial air transport, the Australian data show a statistically significant increase in both occurrence numbers and the rate per million flight hours. The same is true for domestic taxiing collisions and near-collisions.

That does not establish the cause of the recent Sydney events. It does, however, suggest that the longer-term increase in runway incursions and taxiing collisions and near-collisions warrants attention.

Graham Wild is an aviation coordinator at the Australian Defence Force Academy, UNSW.

He is a member of the Royal Aeronautical Society Australian Division, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers.

title: Dolly Parton, music legend, actor, and philanthropist, dies at 80
text:
In brief Legendary musician Dolly Parton has died at 80.

The news was announced by Parton's nephew and representatives via social media.

Dolly Parton, the country music icon whose soaring vibrato vocals, poignant songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, has died. She was 80 years old.

Parton died peacefully in Nashville, Tennessee, her publicist said in a statement released on Wednesday AEST.

Known for her curvy physique, massive blonde wigs and skin-tight outfits that served her self-deprecating wit, she was among the most beloved personalities in music and beyond — the rare celebrity whose appeal transcended generations, geography and politics.

She wrote hundreds of songs, including classics like Jolene, Coat of Many Colours and I Will Always Love You, that totalled more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than one billion online streams.

Parton, who plucked bejewelled banjos, guitars and dulcimers with her long fingernails during performances, was a generous philanthropist and successful businesswoman whose projects included a theme park in the Smoky Mountain foothills near her birthplace.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Her career was forever influenced by her upbringing as one of 12 children born into what she called a "dirt poor" Tennessee family. She started her education nonprofit, Imagination Library, to send free books to children in Tennessee because her father, who quit school to work on the farm, struggled to learn to read.

Parton's first musical performances were in church, where her grandfather was a preacher. By age 10, she was learning guitar and singing on local television shows. At 13, she appeared on the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, where Johnny Cash introduced her as "a little girl here from up in East Tennessee".

With a suitcase of songs, she followed her uncle, Bill Owens, also a songwriter, to Nashville after graduating high school in 1964.

Fred Foster, who produced Roy Orbison, Willie Nelson and more, saw her potential and got her songs cut by other artists, as well as recording and releasing Parton singing her own material. By the mid-1970s, Parton was a Nashville queen.

A key collaboration with Porter Wagoner

Parton's partnership with Porter Wagoner, a pencil-thin pompadoured star with flashy rhinestone outfits, was key to her career. She honed her acting skills on his syndicated TV show, and he advocated for her to get a record deal at RCA. Their first duet, The Last Thing on My Mind, was released in 1967, the same year she started her own publishing company.

While their duets were often big radio hits, Parton's solo singles didn't chart as high at first. With Wagoner as a co-producer, she began to adjust her country warble to a more polished, pop-leaning style.

She got her first No 1 solo single with Joshua, and reached the Top 5 with the ballad Coat of Many Colours, about how her mother sewed together scraps of clothes to make a coat Parton wore "so proudly" even as her peers mocked her for being poor. The song, with its Biblical references and ode to maternal love, was later made into a children’s book and a TV movie.

In 1973, she had the hit that made her career — Jolene, a country music standard with its steady, churning rhythm and Parton's repeated delivery of the title as she pleads for the woman not to steal her man.

The song topped the country charts, crossing over to pop and later being released internationally, opening up new audiences for Parton. Jolene is one of her most covered compositions, including by Miley Cyrus (Parton's goddaughter), Olivia Newton-John and The White Stripes.

She left Wagoner's show in 1974, amid reports of squabbling between the two, although they continued to record together and Wagoner stayed her producer for years after that. But the relationship turned litigious when Wagoner sued her in 1979 for millions in management fees and royalties.

A pop crossover star

She followed Jolene with a huge hit in 1974, I Will Always Love You, an ode and farewell to Wagoner that helped her win the Country Music Association's female vocalist of the year award back-to-back in 1975 and 1976. She famously turned down Elvis Presley, who wanted to record it, because she would not share publishing rights.

Decades later, Whitney Houston's version of I Will Always Love You became a smash for the soundtrack of her 1992 film The Bodyguard, and broke sales records. Houston won a Grammy for her performance in 1994, presented to her by Parton.

Here You Come Again, a pop crossover hit and one of the few she didn't write, further established Parton as a multi-genre entertainer and brought her first Grammy Award in 1979.

Dolly Parton continued to release music and perform throughout her life. Source: Getty / NBCUniversal

"A lot of people thought I had totally lost my mind," she told the Associated Press (AP) in 1979 of changing her singing style. "But I had no fear of change. I expected success, but I was braced for failure. I didn’t care if people thought I was wrong. In my own heart, I knew I was doing the right thing."

Parton's other crossover hits included the title song from 9 to 5, the 1980 comedy starring Parton, Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin; and her duet with longtime friend Kenny Rogers, Islands in the Stream, written by brothers Barry, Maurice and Robin Gibb of the Bee Gees.

In 1987, she collaborated with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris on the million-selling Trio album.

Down home charm

For millions of fans, she was simply "Dolly," a mixture of Southern charm, humour and glamour. But she was also considered a feminist role model for holding the reins of her own career, writing her own songs, owning her content and looking after her finances in an entertainment world dominated by men.

Parton was open to making fun of herself; when she hosted Saturday Night Live in 1989, she told the writers that her only restrictions were that she wouldn't curse and she wouldn't make fun of Jesus. She regularly joked about her breasts or her dumb blonde appearance, but with a wink that she was the one controlling the laughs.

In the memoir My Life So Far, Fonda remembered Parton's way with a wisecrack, "usually high raunch", and a laugh that was "somewhere between a girl's giggle, an explosive shriek, and a cascade of little bells".

After her gown split down the front when she won CMA's entertainer of the year in 1978, Parton quipped: "My daddy said that's what I got for putting 50 pounds of mud in a five-pound bag."

Throughout her career, she embraced her glamorous style, often wearing custom curve-hugging rhinestone dresses and bodysuits even if they drew tsk-tsks from others in the industry. Her look was always a part of her larger musical business plan.

"I knew my songs were good even if I had been ugly as sin," she told the AP in 2014. "So I thought, 'Well, I would have probably chose to look this way even if I had been a waitress.' I mean, this is my look. I mean, I like a lot of makeup. I like a lot of hair. I like flashy clothes. I like to show it off. But that's just who I am."

She married Carl Dean, an asphalt paving contractor, in the mid-1960s; they were together until his death in 2025 at the age of 82. Though rarely seen in public, he was an influence on her career. She told NPR that she wrote Jolene about a flirty bank teller who seemed to take an interest in Dean.

9 to 5 to Hollywood and Broadway

In her first major film role, Parton played alongside Fonda and Tomlin as office workers who rebel against their tyrannical boss in 9 to 5. Critic Roger Ebert called her a "natural-born movie star" and the title song earned her two Grammy Awards and a ranking of 78 on the American Film Institute's list of top 100 movie songs. Starring roles in The Best Little Whorehouse In Texas and Steel Magnolias followed.

Dolly Parton (centre) starred in 9 to 5 alongside Jane Fonda (left) and Lily Tomlin. Source: AAP / AP / Wally Fong

"I never thought of myself as a movie star," she told AP's Bob Thomas in 1979. "I knew I'd be a star, but as a singer or as a writer of songs or books or poetry. I wanted to be a famous performer and wear flashy clothes, but singing in movies was not one of my ambitions. My family lived in the mountains, and we didn't see movies."

Her love affair with TV and film continued for decades, with appearances alongside Cyrus on Hannah Montana and adaptations of her music for Christmas specials, films and streaming series. She also became an author, her books ranging from the memoir Dolly to a bestselling novel co-authored by James Patterson, Run, Rose, Run.

The stage adaptation 9 to 5: The Musical debuted in 2009, and Dolly: A True Original Musical is set to open in December.

United States of Dolly

Beyond her music, Parton’s most lasting legacy might be her generosity and broad appeal.

When a deadly wildfire swept through the Smokies in 2016, she held an all-star telethon and set up a foundation that sent monthly checks to residents whose homes were damaged or destroyed.

She opened Dollywood theme park in East Tennessee, a major economic driver in Appalachia that draws tourists from around the country, and established the Dollywood Foundation.

She wrote books and memoirs, was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame and was given a lifetime achievement award by the Recording Academy. She was selected for the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 2025.

READ MORE How Dolly Parton is fostering a love of reading in children around Australia

With 55 Grammy nominations and 10 wins, Parton is the third-most nominated woman in Grammy history, only behind Beyoncé and Taylor Swift.

Parton spanned social and political divides, through multiple generations of fans, urban and rural and in between. In tumultuous election years, it wasn't uncommon to see "Dolly for President" shirts. But she was strict in not voicing her own political beliefs, often turning aside questions about presidents, candidates, policies and other controversies.

"I don’t do politics," Parton told host Jad Abumrad on his hit podcast Dolly Parton's America.

"I have too many fans on both sides of the fence. Of course, I have my opinion about everything, but I learned years ago to keep your mouth shut about things."

When the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Foundation sent out a ballot in 2022 with her name on it, though she said she felt she hadn't earned it, the voters answered with a "Hello, Dolly".

Parton showed up to the induction ceremony, performed and then put out a rock album.

title: One boat, more than 400 people and 25 years of consequences
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

"We were terrified."

For Farid — a pseudonym used to protect his identity — those three words still carry him back 25 years, to a ship in the Indian Ocean, a teenage boy surrounded by hundreds of strangers, and the sudden arrival of Australian authorities after the vessel that had rescued him was prevented from reaching Christmas Island — an Australian territory.

He was 17. He had fled Afghanistan, leaving behind his single mother and siblings, and spent eight months moving from one boat to another in search of safety.

By the time the Norwegian freighter MV Tampa rescued him and 432 other asylum seekers — most of them Hazara Afghans — from a stricken fishing boat named the Palapa in August 2001, he had already endured storms, days at sea and the uncertainty of not knowing where the journey would end. At the time, Hazaras were fleeing Afghanistan, fearing persecution from the resurgent Taliban.

Then came another uncertainty.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We weren't clearly told where they were going to take us. When we first saw the authorities' ship, I thought they were going to take us to Australia," Farid tells SBS News.

Instead, he was taken to Naoero (formerly known as Nauru), where he would spend years caught up in Australia's newly established offshore processing system before eventually returning to Afghanistan.

"It was like a camp. We get our turns, about once a month, to go out for a few hours," he says.

A refugee settlement seen on Naoero in September 2018. Source: AP / Jason Oxenham

"For the first year we didn't get to go out at all. We were not very hopeful. It was just tents at first, but then they set up portable rooms," Farid says.

Today, he is 42 and lives in Melbourne's south-east, where he works as a painter after completing trade courses and an apprenticeship. He was granted asylum in Australia in 2012.

The ordinary life Farid has built in Australia is a long way from the journey that brought him here, one that began when he was a teenager fleeing Afghanistan and led him into the centre of the 'Tampa crisis' and Australia's emerging offshore processing system.

Twenty-five years on, his experience offers a human window into the events surrounding the Tampa and the policy that followed, known as the Pacific Solution, as Australia continues to debate how it responds to people seeking protection.

When the Tampa answered the call

On 24 August 2001, the Palapa ran into trouble in rough seas about 140km north of Christmas Island, leaving those on board facing the prospect of sinking.

Two days later, on 26 August, Australia's Rescue Coordination Centre alerted ships in the area that the vessel was in distress, with the words "HELP" and "SOS" painted across its roof.

The closest vessel was MV Tampa, whose captain, Arne Rinnan, agreed to come to their aid. Guided by an Australian Coastwatch aircraft, the Tampa reached the stricken fishing boat and began taking those on board to safety.

The Tampa affair unfolded in August 2001, after the vessel rescued 433 asylum seekers from a sinking fishing boat before being prevented from reaching Christmas Island. Source: SBS News

For Farid, the rescue should have marked the end of a terrifying journey. Instead, it was followed by a confrontation that would reshape Australia's approach to asylum seekers arriving by boat.

Rinnan initially headed towards the ferry port of Merak, Indonesia, but several asylum seekers reportedly pressured him to take them to Australia instead. According to a subsequent Senate inquiry, some threatened to jump overboard or hurt themselves if they were taken to Indonesia.

Fearing for their safety, Rinnan changed course for Christmas Island.

Australian authorities refused permission for the vessel to enter Australian territorial waters and directed Rinnan to take those aboard to Indonesia.

The Palapa was carrying more than 400 asylum seekers when it became stranded on 24 August. Source: AAP / Wallenius Wilhelmsen

As the standoff continued, Rinnan raised concerns about the deteriorating health of some passengers.

Australian authorities arranged for food, water, and medical assistance, but the deadlock continued.

On 29 August, Rinnan declared a state of emergency and sailed into Australian waters without permission, prompting the government to send 45 Special Air Service (SAS) troops to board the vessel.

Farid remembers the arrival of the authorities as another moment of fear.

"I was nervous and frightened because they [authorities] wore face coverings and had their fingers on the trigger."

It was like seeing something in the movies. We were confused because the captain explained to us that he was not permitted to enter into Australian waters.

Christmas Island caught in the middle

Gordon Thomson was a Christmas Island Shire councillor at the time and had direct contact with Rinnan during the standoff, including through fax.

Gordon Thomson, a Christmas Island Shire councillor at the time, led a rally calling for the Tampa refugees to be allowed to land on Christmas Island in August 2001. Source: Supplied

On 28 August 2001, Thomson and other elected representatives issued a statement calling on the then-prime minister John Howard to allow the Tampa into the island's port.

"We applaud the captain and crew of the Tampa for their correct application of humanitarian principles and the law in taking onto their ship asylum seekers by offering safe refuge on Christmas Island," the statement read.

But a day later, as the government moved to prevent the Tampa from reaching the island, Thomson says the atmosphere on Christmas Island changed.

"The government brought in the SAS, armed boats and attack craft, effectively taking control of and, in many people's eyes, pirating the Tampa and forcing it back out to sea," he tells SBS News.

"They also closed the port, which meant local people couldn't go out on the water. No-one was allowed to get into a boat, despite fishing being a daily necessity for many people on Christmas Island."

International journalists and news crews gathered on Christmas Island amid intense global interest in the August 2001 Tampa standoff. Source: Supplied

"The government was determined that journalists couldn't get onto boats and reach the Tampa to tell their stories. There was a real clampdown on movement across the island," Thomson says.

With the standoff unresolved, the government turned to an alternative: those aboard would be taken elsewhere, where their claims for protection would be processed.

Life in Naoero

Hassan Ghulam was a community elder in Australia when nearly 300 asylum seekers were transferred to Naoero in September 2001.

Naoero is a tiny Pacific island nation about 3,000km north-east of Australia, and had a population of roughly 12,000 people at the time.

In the weeks after the Tampa crisis, Australia reached an agreement with the Naoero government to establish an offshore processing centre at Topside, in the island's remote interior. In return for hosting the asylum seekers, Naoero received financial and development assistance from Australia.

Community leaders like Hassan Ghulam became crucial links to those on Naoero, advising the Hazara refugees and gathering information about life inside the camp. Source: SBS News / Supplied

The centre was still being built when the first arrivals were sent there, with many initially housed in large tents while Australian personnel worked to establish the facility.

As more asylum seekers arrived, Topside quickly became crowded, with conditions marked by extreme heat, water shortages and limited electricity.

From Australia, people like Ghulam became crucial links to those inside, advising the Hazara refugees and gathering information about life inside the camp from journalists and detainees via satellite phone.

When they were taken on the boat [to Naoero], the conditions were terrible and many suffered from severe physical distress.

"What they endured throughout felt like it was a punishment to scare them into coming into Australia … it was [also] a message intended to the [people] smugglers," Ghulam says.

The now 75-year-old says smugglers charged large sums to put people on boats that were often poorly equipped and unseaworthy, with water sometimes flooding into the vessels as they crossed open seas.

"We Hazaras are mountain people, not sea people," he says.

"If you leave us on a mountainside, we can climb like goats. But in the sea, we are not fish — we would drown."

The first Naoero facility was established rapidly in the aftermath of the crisis, and accounts from the period describe difficult conditions, including shortages of water and other basic services. The island's remoteness also meant limited access to medical care and other support.

Ghulam says he made several attempts to reach Naoero, including one with an Australian documentary news crew hoping to record the conditions inside the detention centre, but they were stopped before they could even board the plane.

Letters from limbo

Instead, detainees began sending Ghulam letters from Naoero — some describing the harsh living conditions, others sharing their hopes for the future, and many reflecting on the pain of being separated from the people they loved.

The letters that made their way from Naoero painted a picture of lives suspended in uncertainty.

In one dated 27 October 2002, a detainee wrote of the ongoing water shortages: "Sometimes God helps us, rain is a great source of water, people come out of containers and take bath in the rain."

They also described the emotional toll of being separated from family: "Normally I do not like to think of my sisters because such feelings make me upset and weak and the circle of life becomes slower here."

SBS News has seen some of the letters, but has not independently verified them in their entirety.

Elaine Smith, an advocacy worker who worked closely on the Tampa affair in Australia at the time, also reviewed copies.

The letters also show some detainees trying to maintain hope despite their circumstances.

One wrote that he did not want to burden the person receiving his letters with his troubles, saying he wanted to "share" his joys.

He described starting a small mathematics class for fellow detainees, while teaching himself English grammar and fiction from the Naoero library.

He said those were among the few subjects available, unlike the mathematics and physics he wanted to study, and asked whether he could pursue further education by distance.

The politics of the Tampa

On 1 September 2001, Howard announced that Naoero and New Zealand had agreed to receive the Tampa passengers for refugee-status processing outside Australia. The arrangement became the foundation of what was later known as the Pacific Solution.

The Tampa's arrival came just weeks before Australia's federal election, which was shaping up around issues including border protection and asylum seekers.

Government figures showed boat arrivals had risen sharply in the years before the Tampa affair — from 921 in 1998-99 to 4,137 in 2000-01. The Howard government argued that Australia was being "targeted by organised people smugglers" because its "refugee determination outcomes were overly generous".

Then-prime minister John Howard poses for a photograph with a couple in the federal seat of Ryan in March 2001, during the federal election year. Source: AAP / Dave Hunt

At the launch of his 2001 election campaign in Sydney, Howard famously delivered a line that would come to define his political legacy on border protection: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."

In a sit-down interview with SBS News 25 years later, he continues to defend his approach and says he reflects positively on his immigration policies.

We were ahead of our time … you couldn't maintain domestic support for strong immigration policies if you allow people to come willy-nilly to live in our country.

"What we adopted was a common sense approach. You cannot maintain local support for high immigration if people feel that the government no longer controls either the number of people or who they are."

Children overboard controversy

The Howard government's hardline approach to boat arrivals reshaped Australia's border policy, but also gave rise to some of the most controversial episodes of the 2001 campaign, including the "children overboard" affair.

The controversy centred on events surrounding SIEV 4, a vessel intercepted by the Australian Navy's HMAS Adelaide on 6 October 2001, about 100 nautical miles north of Christmas Island.

The following day, 7 October, a report emerged that asylum seekers had thrown children overboard as the Navy attempted to intercept the vessel. A subsequent Senate inquiry found no children had been thrown overboard from SIEV 4.

On 8 October, SIEV 4 started to sink while under tow, and photographs taken during the rescue were later presented as evidence associated with the alleged incident.

The inquiry found the photographs had been wrongly associated with the "children overboard" claim.

Howard has previously defended his handling of the affair, saying he relied on the advice he received at the time. In 2002, he told ABC Lateline he had never been told the original advice was wrong. Twenty years later, in an interview with the Guardian, he again defended the claims, saying: "It was the advice we had at the time."

Former prime minister John Howard told SBS News there had been a "miscommunication" in the advice he received during the "children overboard" controversy. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

But in his interview with SBS News 25 years on, Howard offers a somewhat different characterisation of the episode.

That was a mistake, that was a miscommunication.

"I don't think anybody is to be blamed for that," he says.

He says the reaction was understandable given the "enormous turmoil" and emotion of the time, before shifting focus to what he sees as the policy's longer-term outcome.

"All I can say is it's good we are not having accidents at sea now, like we used to have then."

The legacy of 'stopping the boats'

Howard's reference to "accidents at sea" points to the deadly period of boat arrivals that followed the Tampa affair.

In December 2010, 50 people died when SIEV 221, carrying asylum seekers, crashed into the rocky shoreline of Christmas Island in treacherous seas — a tragedy the WA coroner later described as the largest loss of life in an Australian maritime incident in peacetime in 115 years.

It was one of a series of boat journeys in the years that followed, with hundreds of asylum seekers dying at sea as boats attempted to reach Australia.

A protest sign on Christmas Island calling for the Tampa refugees to be allowed to land, reading: "Let the Tampa refugees land." Source: Supplied

Since December 2013, the Australian government has reported no known deaths at sea from maritime people-smuggling ventures targeting Australia.

Howard views that outcome as evidence that Australia's approach was ultimately vindicated — and argues that other countries are now confronting similar challenges.

We were right and the rest of the world is adopting our approach.

Howard says the position he took during the 2001 election was criticised at the time, particularly by some Europeans who regarded it as insensitive. But, he argues, many of those same countries are now grappling with the challenges of irregular migration and border control.

"You can't have an open, tolerant, non-discriminatory immigration policy if it's open slather," he says.

"You can't. And we decided a long time ago. And the rest of the world is now adopting the approach we adopted then."

The challenges Howard describes remain evident across Europe. On 21 August, French police were filmed intercepting an inflatable boat as migrants attempted to cross the English Channel to Britain, part of an intensified effort to prevent small-boat departures.

At the end of July, thousands of people tried to cross from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, in a mass influx that resulted in dozens of deaths.

Asked how he would judge his own legacy on immigration and border protection, Howard declines to do so himself.

"That's for other people. I cannot be my own judge. Others will be my judge.

"I think we ran an immigration policy that most Australians support, one that still allows us to adopt a humanitarian approach."

The debate over 'stopping the boats'

Graham Thom, advocacy coordinator at the Refugee Council of Australia, acknowledges immigration is a complex issue, but disagrees offshore processing was responsible for 'stopping the boats'.

"One of the key myths that is very difficult to dispel is that somehow offshore processing stops the boats from arriving," he tells SBS News.

Graham Thom, advocacy coordinator at the Refugee Council of Australia, says offshore processing has not stopped people arriving by boat. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

"There's this whole narrative around 'stopping the boats', when what we saw after Tampa was the Howard government starting to intercept boats and push them back," Thom says.

Tampa didn't stop the boats. People kept coming.

"Until we acknowledge that the Pacific Solution had nothing to do with stopping the boats, we're sort of trapped in a system that has bipartisan support for cruelty."

Thom says Australia should instead work with countries across the region, including Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, to ensure people have basic rights, access to work and study, and protection from detention or removal while longer-term solutions are found.

"[We] don't need to resettle everyone," he says.

"As long as there is hope that those most at risk can get to some sort of safety, then you remove the incentive for people to get on dangerous boat journeys."

When asked about critics who argue that the arrival of asylum seekers by boat is not Australia's responsibility, Thom says the issue needs to be considered as part of a broader global system.

"I say to any critic, we are part of a global system and we have to look at our responsibility globally.

"If we don't solve the problem at its source, people are going to keep moving, and they will keep moving until they find safety and security.

Demonising, criminalising and isolating people is not the solution.

Thom says the debate over border protection has continued to shape how migration is discussed in Australia.

Protesters dressed as SAS troops mark the second anniversary of the Tampa affair at a rally in Melbourne in 2003. Source: AAP / Joe Castro

"I think the whole migration debate is blowing up on all proportions and it is always easy when times are tough to blame someone … and migrants are often first to face those attacks," Thom says.

"Ultimately, how we treat them is a reflection of us, not a reflection of people trying to seek a better life."

Howard rejects that characterisation of his approach. He says he hadn't been concerned with how the decision might be viewed 25 years later; he was thinking of "what's right at the time" and that "we had to say no".

"We have a proud record of taking people in from all around the world and a generous humanitarian program.

"We wanted to maintain that."

Life after Tampa

But Naoero was not the end of Farid's story. His asylum application was rejected and he was eventually returned to Afghanistan, where he lived for eight years before being granted asylum and returning to Australia in 2012.

Today Farid is a painter, but his hopes of pursuing a career as an educator have not disappeared.

Since leaving Afghanistan, he has helped establish a primary school of 320 students in his old village, a dream he has relished, having grown up determined that no other child in his community would have to travel hours to reach the nearest school.

Farid's life now straddles two places: the community he left behind in Afghanistan and the life he has built in Australia. His experience offers a personal lens into a question at the heart of Australia's migration debate: what does it mean to become Australian?

Howard views it differently, rejecting the idea that Australia's identity needs to be defined as either "mono" or multicultural.

"It's all pointless. I don't think we should fret about definition, what it is.

The thing is, migration to Australia since World War Two has been a huge success.

"[But] what we should not do is ignore people who want greater control over immigration. They want a ceiling on the number of people who come here, and they don't want people who aren't willing to adopt our ways coming here. How you enforce those two things is a matter of debate."

title: 'You can't escape': A growing fight over what belongs in Australia's suburbs
text:
In Brief New federal government rules will ban future data centres from being built near homes and schools.

But residents living alongside them say they've been left out and feel powerless.

When Sean Brown moved to West Footscray two years ago, days after his son was born, he thought he'd found a good spot to raise a family — green space, a train station nearby, and a community with room to grow.

Instead, his home is now 300 metres from one of the largest data centres in the country.

"It's a massive black box in the middle of a residential area. There's this visual heaviness to it that you can't really escape," Brown told SBS News.

NextDC's M3 facility in the Melbourne suburb brings a constant humming noise audible even 100m away, he said, while ongoing construction means near-constant light, noise and disruption.

Parking is scarce with facility workers competing for street spots, and Brown said whole streets have lost power for full days at a time during infrastructure works, with little warning and no compensation. He's also worried about health risks, and the future of his entire suburb.

Sean Brown lives 300m away from one of Australia's biggest data centres. Source: Supplied

Branded by its chief executive, Craig Scroggie, as "Australia's largest hyperscale AI factory", the M3 site is set to double in size by 2027 — covering 10 hectares in size, and drawing 225MW of power, 24 hours a day.

A separate facility, the Perri Melbourne Data Centre (PMDC), has been approved and planned just a few blocks over.

There are currently 162 operational data centres across Australia, with a further 90 proposed, according to the Climate Council — and it's unclear whether planned rules to data centres in residential areas will apply to any of them.

In the streets of West Footscray surrounded by houses, a "massive black box" has taken over. Source: Supplied / Sean Brown

Government crackdown on new data centres

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used a speech to the Business Council of Australia's annual dinner on Tuesday night to announce new national rules that would block future data centres from being built near homes, schools, or prime agricultural land.

READ MORE The new plan to prevent data centres from driving power prices up

Developers will also be required to add more renewable energy to the grid than their data centres consume, minimise water use, and ensure new sites are appropriate for their size — avoiding land that could otherwise be used for housing.

"Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential," Albanese said.

"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained and locations are appropriate."

Asked about communities already living with data centres, Albanese did not directly answer when pressed on ABC Perth on Tuesday, instead pointing to the same social licence framework.

Asked by SBS News whether any measures would target existing sites or address community concern that the new rules don't cover people already affected, the prime minister's office declined to comment.

NextDC's M3 data centre is set for an expansion that will cover 10 hectares of West Footscray, while another separate facility, the Perri Melbourne Data Centre (PMDC) has been approved just a few blocks over. Source: Supplied / Sean Brown

A big gap

While Brown welcomes the changes in principle, he said they don't reach the people already living with the consequences.

"If it doesn't fix the problems that have been caused in West Footscray, what's the point of it?" Brown said. "This community's just been completely sold down the river if we're not looked after. Why do our children continue to bear this risk?"

He's sceptical that the sites would have been approved under the new government frameworks and said it needs to expand to existing data centres, not just the new ones.

"If areas where they've already been inappropriately built are just left to fend for themselves, how is that fair at all?"

Associate Professor Dr Ehsan Noroozinejad, a researcher at the Urban Transformations Research Centre at Western Sydney University, welcomed the government's changes but said a clear gap remained.

"The proposed rules mainly shape future development, so they do not automatically resolve concerns around existing facilities," he told SBS News.

The M3 site is set to double in size by 2027 — covering 10 hectares in size, and drawing 225MW of power, 24 hours a day. Source: Supplied / Sean Brown

"Communities already living near data centres need clear standards for noise, water use, backup generators, traffic and energy impacts, backed by transparent monitoring."

Noroozinejad said Australia still needs data centres, but problems arise when they aren't put in the right places with the right infrastructure.

"It's important not to assume every data centre creates the same problems," he said. "The real issue is performance, location, and whether costs are shifted onto the surrounding community."

Dr Michael Vardon, from the Fenner School of Environment and Society at Australian National University, said the deeper problem is procedural: communities have almost no input before a facility is approved.

"This is about where new facilities go, and setback rules do not apply retrospectively," Vardon told SBS News.

"The approval comes first, the community finds out afterwards, and by then the only remaining policy lever is the operating conditions."

A view of NextDC's M3 data centre from Kendal Coombs' house. Source: Supplied / Kendal Coombs

Olivia Shen, director of the strategic technologies program with the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney, said a key provision of the changes will be whether they apply to both expansion of existing data centres as well as new projects.

"Many data centres have operated in Australia for decades, often without the surrounding community even realising they are there," Shen told SBS News. "However, if existing data centres are allowed to expand to a point where they encroach on homes, schools and agricultural land, then this becomes a bit of a policy loophole."

'We feel really powerless'

Another West Footscray resident, Kendal Coombs, bought a house four years ago about 200 metres from the M3 site, when the block was still vacant.

She said she was initially told by council that the site was going to be a "business park", but realised a few months after moving in that it was a data centre — which was initially not a concern until its rapid expansion.

"We're all angry and concerned but it's hard to know what to do, we feel really powerless," she said.

"These projects destroy communities. If they're making these determinations [that future data centres can't be built near homes or schools] because it is too unsafe or too much of a risk to our health to live near them, then they need to pay reparations to the residents affected."

Brown said the centres have made it harder to sell up and leave.

"There's a lot of people here who are really angry about what impact this is going to have on their house prices — because I sure as hell wouldn't live near a data centre," he said. "I wouldn't buy this house."

He's pushing for compensation: voluntary housing buybacks at competitive market rates for those who no longer want to live there, relocation costs covered for owners and renters alike, and payment for disruption already endured.

NextDC has not responded to these proposals, Brown says, adding government intervention is needed.

Both Noroozinejad and Vardon say more transparency and reporting is needed for existing data centres in neighbourhoods — particularly information around water and energy use, noise, independent monitoring, and a complaints register.

Practical measures such as acoustic upgrades, landscaping, traffic management and limits on backup-generator testing can also help, Noroozinejad said.

But for Brown, it might be too late.

"They've just killed this area now," he said. "We're witnessing the death of a suburb."

NextDC declined to comment.

title: 'Extraordinarily expensive': Is this Australia's most controversial construction project?
text:
In brief Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says changes to the Suburban Rail Loop will mean it is "built under budget".

There has been division over the infrastructure project's costs, with the state Opposition vowing to review it if elected.

Few infrastructure projects have generated as much debate as Victoria's Suburban Rail Loop.

The 90km rail project promises to reshape how Melbourne grows and moves, but its cost, benefits and delivery timeline have been fiercely contested.

That debate has again been thrust into the spotlight after Premier Ben Carroll announced $2 billion in cuts to the project this week, declaring: "I respect your money."

Supporters say the rail loop is a once-in-a-generation investment that will help accommodate Melbourne's growth. But critics argue it comes with an eye-watering price tag and uncertain returns, helping make it one of Australia's most controversial infrastructure projects.

Liam Davies, a lecturer in sustainability and urban planning at RMIT University, said the SRL was a step towards transforming Melbourne's city-centric public transport system into an interconnected network.
