Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Melbourne's greatest challenge is that it has become an extraordinarily large city, physically," he told SBS News.

"We can't just adopt the transport strategy for a denser, more compact city like London. We need to do something of our own, and the SRL is an attempt to do that in a Melburnian context."

With Labor and the Coalition deeply divided on the SRL, the project's future could be decided when Victorians head to the polls in November.

Why is the project so controversial?

The SRL will connect Melbourne's middle suburbs from Cheltenham in the south-east to Werribee in the west via Melbourne Airport through a 90km underground rail line.

The project is split into three stages. The first section — SRL East — is under construction, running from Cheltenham to Box Hill via six new underground stations. The first trains are expected by 2035.

Critics argue the mega-project's business case doesn't stack up, and the multi-billion-dollar price tag is a financial liability for Victoria, which has the second-highest debt per capita of any state or territory, behind the Northern Territory.

The project's first stage, SRL East, in Melbourne's south-east is well underway. Source: Supplied / Victorian government

More than $33 billion has already been invested in SRL East, according to the premier.

A Parliamentary Budget Office analysis puts the price tag for building the East and North sections at $96.4 billion, though there is currently no fully costed estimate for the entire project, which includes the final stage, SRL West.

An evaluation last year by Infrastructure Australia — an advisory body to the federal government — found the SRL's business case was insufficiently detailed and relied on future stages to justify its benefits.

It also urged the Victorian government to develop "exit strategies" should the project be unable to be completed.

Allegations of corruption and unlawful conduct in state-funded projects, which recently led to a royal commission into the construction industry being called, have also heightened public concerns about the SRL.

Davies said there are questions about which other infrastructure projects will miss out on investment because of the SRL.

"This is still an extraordinarily expensive project," he said.

"Is this the only project that we build over the next 35 to 50 years, or do we build other projects at the same time?

"If it's the only project that we build, I don't think it's the best allocation of resources."

Are there alternatives?

Carroll, who replaced Jacinta Allan as premier last month, has clearly recognised that many Victorians are unhappy with the eye-watering cost.

On Tuesday, he announced $2 billion in savings, with underground station interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley no longer to be built, instead replaced by surface transfers.

Among other changes, a second station entrance will not be built at Clayton, and pedestrian bridges in Burwood and Cheltenham have also been axed.

"I respect your money," Carroll said in a statement.

"The SRL will be built on time. Today's changes mean it will be built under budget."

Davies said construction of SRL East was well advanced, with tunnel boring machines in place to begin excavating twin 26km tunnels.

"The reality is that that project is so far along; it will continue," he said.

But it's the project's latter stages which have scope for change.

Davies said better rail services and upgrades to the northern and western suburb lines, including electrification of the entire track, would fulfil many of the policy ambitions of SRL West at a fraction of the time and cost.

"We have an exploding population in our northern and western suburbs, and the infrastructure is not keeping up at all," he said.

He said there could also be alternatives to the SRL North, such as elevated rail, light rail, or a rapid bus transit system with dedicated bus lanes.

"There are challenges to each of those options; each of them has trade-offs," he said.

"All of them would be cheaper options than what we currently have, which is tens of billions of dollars in tunnelling."

Where do the parties stand?

The project's future could hinge on the outcome of the state's November election.

Labor has committed to seeing the SRL through, arguing it's essential infrastructure for a growing Melbourne.

The state Opposition has previously called for the project to be scrapped, arguing that it's too costly and the funds should be redirected to other, higher-priority transport projects, such as a long-sought-after airport line.

In 2024, Liberal MLC Evan Mulholland described the SRL as a "vanity project" that was "robbing the next generation of getting the infrastructure that they deserve".

But the Coalition's position has evolved over time, with Opposition leader Jess Wilson now promising to pause and review the project if elected.

Whatever the outcome, the project will remain a defining political issue for years to come.

"Transport projects are big and expensive, and they almost always have controversy," Davies said.

"It's almost impossible to build something that everyone is going to be absolutely happy with. Maybe this is just another example of that."

title: 'Get it out': ARIA to ban AI-generated music from Australian charts
text:
In brief ARIA will ban fully AI-generated music from featuring on its charts from Friday.

Australian artists like Peking Duk's Adam Hyde have welcomed the move.

Music will need to be "substantially human-made" in order to qualify for Australia's main music chart, in an industry bid to stamp out AI-generated tracks.

Songs wholly generated using artificial intelligence will no longer be eligible for the ARIA charts from Friday, in an update to The Australian Recording Industry Association's (ARIA) code of practice.

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would "undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to present".

"The ARIA charts are about tracking consumption and sales of music in Australia, but they're also about celebrating human artistry and success," Herd told ABC radio.

"We're not particularly interested in including AI-generated music as part of that process, particularly when it's taking up a spot from an Australian artist in the chart."

AI-assisted songs will still feature on the charts, but they must be substantially human-made and raise no stream or chart manipulation concerns.

"I'm sure that there are a lot of artists that are using AI tools to enhance creativity, to do really cool, new, exciting things," Herd said.

"Artists have always been at the forefront of new tech ... it's made some of the best music ever created, and no doubt AI will create some really exciting evolution of that."

Songs on the ARIA charts that use AI include Gold Coast-based DJ and producer Josh Fawaz's dance track Like a Prayer, which is fourth on the ARIA's top 20 Australian singles after peaking at number two in May.

A dance cover of Madonna's 1989 hit, generative AI is credited for the drums and vocals on the track, according to Spotify.

Australian electronic band Peking Duk supported the association's call to outlaw generative AI from the charts, claiming it was "removing the human experience from life".

"AI is using our stuff. It's using a lot of our peers' stuff, you know, people we know," band member Adam Hyde told Channel Nine's Today show.

"There is so much good art in Australia and something like AI coming along and kind of sweeping the charts and all that jazz, it's like, get it out."

ARIA's decision heeds global AI principles drawn up by the record industry's peak body, The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, in July.

The federation said the guidelines would be rolled out to official charts in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia and advocated to more than 20 other official chart programs in Europe and the Pacific, including the ARIAs.

title: Trump's visa crackdown plan could affect thousands seeking asylum in the US
text:
In brief The US government is set to revoke business and tourism visas for foreigners seeking asylum.

If enacted, it would be the largest mass revocation of visas in US history.

The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States.

If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.

Unless challenged or revised, the US state department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to state department documents obtained by the Associated Press (AP) and two US officials. The action will be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," state department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said.

He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis".

The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.

Since US President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds to process visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.

In a social media post on Tuesday, US deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the US and then apply for asylum.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau said in a post on X. "Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the US in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.

B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the US and would be affected by the revocations.

Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the US and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.

In the past 18 months, the state department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East.

The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the US to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship.

Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the US Supreme Court.

The state department documents obtained by AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the state department received information about asylum requests from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

title: A common tax misconception could catch some Australians by surprise
text:
In brief When does selling your unwanted items on Marketplace go from hobby to business?

When do you actually need to start declaring your earnings from Marketplace?

It’s now easier than ever to sell your unwanted clothes or household items online in Australia. Many popular sites, from eBay, Depop, Facebook Marketplace to newly arrived competitors like Vinted, have either scrapped or limited their seller’s fees, depending on the location, value and number of items sold.

So when do you need to declare your online sales income to the Australian Taxation Office and pay tax on it?

The answer can be as messy as your wardrobe. Be aware there is no minimum value of sales that triggers taxation obligations in Australia.

Digging into the law reveals key questions to consider whether you’re spring cleaning your wardrobe to get some cash for the latest fashion, selling a more valuable asset, or starting to run a business.

Tracking 600 million transactions a year

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Two of the biggest online sales sites, eBay and Amazon, are required to provide lots of transaction data to the tax office.

What about selling goods on other platforms? The tax office may be tracking that too. Its tentacles are vast, with more than 600 million transactions reported and matched to taxpayers every year from a wide variety of private and public sources.

Even if a platform is not required to report, the transactions may still be captured through credit and debit card payment systems, such as Stripe or Square.

The tax office can also request information from the banks. It may even gather information via insurers on unexplained wealth based on "lifestyle assets" – such as cars, boats or art – you may own. There are also examples of taxpayers being caught out with unexplained deposits leading to hefty tax bills.

Is it just a hobby?

Let’s say you found a dress in your wardrobe that you bought for A$250, wore once, but don’t like. So you decide to sell it on eBay or Amazon, rather than giving it away.

You list it and sell it for $100. While you’ve now got $100 more than before, you have really lost $150 overall.

This is not a sound business model. Anything you sell actually comes at a cost to you; think profit, not just sales.

The tax office is unlikely to be interested in these types of occasional, low-value, generally loss-making personal-type activities.

In this scenario, where you’re just cashing in on your existing wardrobe, the tax office is likely to consider it private in nature and just a "hobby".

This is unlikely to create a tax bill. However, you still may need to declare certain activity and have records to support your position.

When does online selling become a business?

What happens when you go from selling just a few old dresses to spotting a market opportunity? Perhaps you start to develop a pattern of buying vintage clothes from friends, family and op shops and selling them at a markup?

Now you’re putting in time and money with the aim of making a profit.

That sort of activity makes it more likely for the tax office to see it as a "business".

A business typically involves repeated and continuous activities. For example, regularly buying items to resell online for profit would be more likely to be considered a business.

Another factor to consider is how systematic you are being. Are you acting in a "business-like" manner? For example, the kind of records you keep, and whether you advertise beyond family and friends, will both be relevant.

No minimum sales to be a business

While the value of sales can be a factor, be careful, as there is no clear dollar threshold for when activities will be considered a business.

But what data the tax office collects from eBay and Amazon provides a clue as to when you’re more likely to be asked questions. Amazon and eBay both share data for people who sell goods worth a total of A$12,000 or more in a particular year.

Earning more or less than that amount does not rule you in or out of running a business, and whether your activities are taxable or not. But if you are earning more than $12,000, you will be on the radar of the tax office – and more likely to be asked to explain your activities.

If you are running a business, you will need to declare income and can claim allowable expenses. You need to pay tax on the net business income.

Consider other tax obligations too. For instance, do you need an Australian Business Number (ABN)? Should you register for the goods and services tax (GST)? If you’re unsure, the federal government’s business website has useful resources.

When in doubt, get advice

Even if you only sell online occasionally, the tax office may be more interested if it involves higher valued goods — such as jewellery originally purchased for more than $500, or other personal items purchased for more than $10,000 – which you’re now trying to sell.

For these more valuable sales, any gain you make – if you managed to sell it for more than you originally paid – is taxable.

However, it gets a little murky if you have made a loss. In general, the tax office restricts how to use losses for these higher valued personal items.

If you’re still unsure whether your online selling is just a hobby, if you’re about to sell a valuable asset, or think you might have crossed over into running a business, don’t risk it — speak to a registered tax practitioner for advice.

title: 'Alarm bells': How Australia ended up back where it started
text:
in brief Fewer than 40 per cent of 25-34-year-olds were listed as homeowners in the 2021 Census, and has reached 1940s levels.

Anglicare Australia would like to see policy settings shift to support younger Australians aspiring to home ownership.

The number of younger Australians who own their own homes has stagnated, sitting at around the same levels recorded during World War Two, as the cost of living and rents rise.

Fewer than 40 per cent of 25 to 34-year-olds were listed as homeowners in the 2021 Census, and that rate is expected to have fallen since, according to analysis from social welfare charity Anglicare Australia.

This is equivalent to the homeownership rate recorded in the 1940s, before the post-war boom took hold as multiple policies prioritised construction and housing for veterans.

At the same time, home prices and rents have risen, putting pressure on younger Australians to save for a mortgage while living away from home.

A recent report from property data company Cotality has shown that rents in some parts of Australia have soared by 80 per cent over the last five years, since COVID-era rent freezes were lifted.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Anglicare Australia said that support lines for younger people are dominated by stress over housing security and related bills.

"It's almost impossible to have a call from a younger person who doesn’t mention the stress of rents or bills," Anglicare Australia executive director Kasy Chambers told SBS News.

"They are studying, working and contributing. But they are earning less than the generations before them, being locked out of housing, and struggling to build the security that past generations took for granted."

Home ownership has steadily declined across age groups since the 1970s, but younger Australians have felt the sharpest declines, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Source: SBS News

Angela Jackson, an economist at the Productivity Commission, the Australian government's independent economic advisory body, said home ownership is particularly hard for lower socioeconomic groups.

"It is a lot more expensive relative to people's incomes to get into the housing market than it was for Gen Z's parents or grandparents," she told SBS News.

"Which does raise alarm bells about broader equity."

Housing in the 1940s

Home ownership rates have declined generation on generation in Australia, off the back of the housing boom in the post-war era.

Liz Allen, a demographer and social researcher from ANU, described 1940s Australians as going through "tough times".

"There were issues with inequalities, especially around education, geographic and income and wealth inequality," she said.

"I think it would be fair to say that the inequalities faced in that period and the global shocks during that period surpassed those that we're experiencing now."

Home ownership across all ages was lower than it is today, with younger people aged 25-34 the least likely to own property.

Allen said that the years after World War Two saw the "rhetoric of a fair go", where government made a non-partisan effort to "rebuild Australia".

It was a time of rapid residential construction and increases in home ownership.

"There were policies on multiple fronts to get people to Australia, to get people in Australia in work, in paid work, and to get people established in life with good wellbeing, access to education, homes, and so on," she said.

"But now we've lost our way."

Allen said that decades of governments have shifted towards short-term policy wins, and "kicked the can" of long-term housing "down the road".

"We're no longer in that mentality of building, but maintaining," she said.

"And that undermines the very notion that we are a growing population, that we have new forms of inequalities emerging, and policy has not kept with societal and economic change."

Less secure work

For many Australians, a home and the equity it generates over time will be their largest source of wealth and a source of security for children who may subsequently inherit it.

But for younger generations who take longer to save and pay off a home, the economic benefits can be diminished.

Jackson explained that the nature of work also makes it harder for Gen Zs to earn like their parents and grandparents.

READ MORE Young Australians may keep pace with their parents — but a deeper wealth rift is emerging

"Work is more casual and can be more gig work, or less secure, which can make entering into mortgages and those long-term financial arrangements more difficult," she said.

"And then incomes themselves have changed over time. For lower entry-level jobs compared to more experienced jobs, the relative wage is also lower."

Rentals out of reach

Anglicare Australia would like to see policy settings shift to support younger Australians aspiring to home ownership.

"The government has taken an important step by reforming property tax breaks that have favoured accumulated wealth over work. Now we need to build on that progress," Chambers said.

"One of the clearest places to start is Youth Allowance.

"We have a social security system that literally says a young person needs less money to live on simply because of their age. Our findings show they can’t afford rent on Youth Allowance anywhere in the country."

Source: SBS News

The government recently announced a $20.90 increase to the maximum Youth Allowance payment due to indexation, which will reach $1,087.20 in September. However the rate can be much lower depending on your age, living situation and dependents.

Meanwhile, the median weekly unit rent in Australia is just under $700, putting rentals out of reach for Youth Allowance recipients.

"Rent isn’t cheaper when you’re 23. Groceries aren’t cheaper. Electricity isn’t cheaper. Yet young people are expected to survive on the lowest payment in the system," Chambers added.

The group would also like to see a wealth tax, which could tax assets and reduce the pressure on income-reliant Australians who don’t yet own a home.

title: 130,000 or 230,000? The migration figures One Nation is trying to explain
text:
in brief One Nation MPs presented conflicting figures regarding their proposed annual net overseas migration targets.

Party leader Pauline Hanson clarified that the official policy remains a strict cap of 130,000.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has faced questions over his party's immigration target, claiming fellow MP David Farley misspoke when he revealed their figures were "not too different" from Labor's.

The MP for Farrer told ABC's Insiders program on Sunday that One Nation's stated figure of 130,000 net overseas migration annually into Australia did not include those who enter under a Pacific labour scheme, aged-care nurses, and other in-demand skilled workers.

He conceded that those groups would add roughly 100,000 people, bringing their total to 230,000 — 5,000 fewer than the current Labor budget projections.

Party leader Pauline Hanson intervened just hours later, writing on social media that One Nation's policy is to reduce net overseas migration (NOM) to 130,000.

Speaking to Channel Seven's Sunrise program on Monday, Joyce added that Farley simply made a mistake while explaining the numbers.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Show me a political career where people haven't made a mistake, and I'll show you a person who's not told the truth," Joyce said.

"I'm not going to throw anybody under a bus. When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that's what happens. God knows, I've done it enough."

The debate over Australia's migration figures has intensified in recent months, with a recent Redbridge/Accent Research poll, conducted for the Australian Financial Review, indicating that voters trust One Nation and its traditionally restrictive approach to handle migration better than Labor or the Liberal Party.

However, the disjointed nature of One Nation's ongoing public discourse on the topic has prompted claims that the party is "incoherent" and "not fit to govern" from federal minister Pat Conroy.

What is One Nation's immigration target?

Since its 1997 inception, cutting immigration has been seemingly a foundational pillar of One Nation policy. During her first speech to federal parliament, Hanson alleged Australia was in danger of being "swamped by Asians", that migrants never assimilated, and that multiculturalism should be abolished.

Its website currently states One Nation would "cut immigration by over 570,000 people" through "capping visas at 130,000 per year".

In a social media post on Sunday, Hanson wrote that NOM would be cut to 130,000 — a figure the party has previously clarified to SBS News. This number would be achieved by reducing international students, temporary graduate visas, and a "much more targeted" skilled migration program, Hanson said.

One Nation member for Farrer David Farley (right) has said the party's immigration target would actually be 100,000 more than initially suggested. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

Those figures are different to the ones put forward by Farley, who said One Nation is focusing on "the NOM in its true form", as separate to labour programs "that drive our economy".

"The raw number is not too different [to current projections], but the reality is, where do we need them?" he asked.

"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."

Joyce further affirmed Hanson's view that One Nation's policy remained at 130,000 people annually for NOM.

SBS News has contacted One Nation for comment.

Where do Labor and the Coalition stand on immigration?

NOM hit 306,000 in the 2024-2025 period, down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000.

Labor is yet to unveil its plan to restrict migration, but has previously set an official cap of 185,000 places on the permanent migration program. Treasury figures project that NOM will fall to 225,000 by the 2027-28 financial year.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was set to detail Labor's plan to ensure that forecast was met, but pulled out of a National Press Club address at the last minute over fears about the implications cuts would have for certain sectors.

"Our policy will be released when Tony Burke is in a position to do so," Conroy told ABC Radio National on Monday. "But we've been very focused on getting the right migration mix to grow the economy as well as the broader interests of Australia."

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has said the Coalition will cap NOM at or below the number of homes built in Australia the previous year. Current building rates suggest their figure would be under 180,000; however, the Coalition is yet to announce where they would restrict immigration to reach that figure.

Opposition immigration spokesperson Jonathon Duniam told ABC Radio National that the Coalition is being "fairly methodical" in assessing its figures but that he would not "put a date" on when it will reveal details.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce (right) said David Farley was mistaken when he said the party's targets did not include essential workers. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

Duniam attacked One Nation for being cavalier with its migration figures, saying it had not detailed the impact such reductions would have on industries like agriculture, which relies on working holiday visa holders for seasonal labour.

"It was the same leader of One Nation who said in an interview about a week ago as well that she did not care about the impact on business any change to the migration system would have," Duniam said.

What's in a NOM?

NOM is difficult for governments to control because it is a measurement of human behaviour rather than a fixed quota.

NOM is calculated by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) based on the movement of people, subtracting overseas departures from overseas arrivals. To be included, a person must remain in the country for any 12 out of 16 months.

Citizens, permanent residents, temporary visa holders, and asylum seekers are included, as are backpackers and working holiday makers who stay for more than a year.

In 2024-2025, 568,000 people entered Australia, according to the ABS, down 14 per cent on the previous year.

Of that cohort, 88,000 were permanent visa holders, 53,000 were New Zealand citizens, and 64,000 were returning Australians. At the same time, 263,000 people left the country.

As Hanson stated, "short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration".

However, using Farley's figures, many of the 100,000 additional workers he says would be able to enter the country — such as workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme — would be included in NOM.

PALM workers can enter under a short-term placement of up to nine months or a long-term placement of one to four years.

The visa caps One Nation plans to set would place policy restrictions on NOM, but they can't control it entirely. Australians suddenly returning home en masse from abroad would, for example, elevate the figure regardless of visa caps.

Migration experts have long cautioned that linking migration to housing shortages is a flawed argument and that, in fact, migrant workers are essential to increase housing stock.

"If we don't have workers doing the jobs we need, if we don't get the right skill set into our country, then we all are worse off," Duniam said.

"One Nation has zero regard for that, as evidenced by the multiple positions they've had on migration policy all over the last few weeks."

title: The hidden underbelly of Australia's weight-loss drug boom
text:
This article contains references to eating disorders.

For Kansasin Darwan, living in Bajool in central Queensland, the weight-loss injection was supposed to be a solution. Instead, she says, it left her barely able to function.

I was dizzy, nauseous, and I lost my appetite. To put it simply, I could barely live.

The 48-year-old says she had gained weight during perimenopause and believed her Australian GP was unlikely to prescribe a weight-management medicine because she did not meet the relevant clinical criteria.

In Australia, GLP-1 weight loss drugs are generally prescribed for chronic weight management in adults with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, or a BMI of 27 to under 30 with at least one weight-related health condition.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

So, while on holiday in her home country of Thailand, Darwan went to a beauty clinic in outer Bangkok and bought an injectable medicine branded as Mounjaro.

Beauty clinics in Thailand are generally supervised by doctors. However, the screening process for GLP-1 use can be less extensive than the assessment typically conducted by GPs in Australia. For example, some customers at beauty clinics may be prescribed GLP-1 drugs even if they do not have diabetes or are within a healthy weight range.

Darwan brought the drugs back to Australia and began using them to lose weight.

"I couldn't concentrate while driving. I wasn't feeling like myself. I couldn't sleep. Even my children noticed that I was different," she tells SBS Thai.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration has issued multiple safety advisories regarding the importation of unregistered GLP-1 products promoted online for weight loss. Source: PA / Niall Carson

Eighteen out of every 1,000 Australians, or almost 2 per cent of the population, are now taking GLP-1s regularly, according to a study by scientists at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) published in November 2025.

Darwan's experience offers a glimpse into a fast-growing market for weight-loss injections, where some Australians are seeking access overseas, while others are obtaining medicines through social-media sellers and informal supply channels.

An investigation by SBS Thai found weight-loss medicines being offered without a doctor's prescription in Australian community groups, reports of products entering the country through informal channels, and unapproved peptides being marketed as weight-loss products.

But access to these medicines is not uniformly occurring outside the established medical system. Many Australians obtain weight-loss drugs through registered health professionals and pharmacies.

For consumers navigating this market, the distinction between an approved prescription medicine, an experimental drug and an unapproved product can be difficult to see — with experts and authorities warning that using medicines outside approved pathways can carry serious risks.

The unregulated supply chain

For some consumers, access does not require a trip overseas.

SBS Thai found GLP-1 injectable medicines openly advertised in Australian Thai community Facebook groups, with some sellers offering the products without requiring a prescription.

We contacted one Melbourne-based seller, posing as a potential customer interested in buying "Mounjaro". The seller offered a 5mg vial for $750, saying it had been sourced from a beauty clinic in Udon Thani, a provincial city in north-east Thailand.

We contacted the clinic identified by the seller, which confirmed that it supplied products to the Melbourne-based seller.

SBS Thai has not independently established the circumstances of every shipment or whether every product sold through the channel was imported in accordance with Australian requirements.

The price for the 5mg multi-dose pre-filled injection pen also appeared significantly higher than the price we found for the same branded medicine at Australian pharmacies, where it was listed between $375 and $415 depending on the pharmacy and required a prescription.

The seller's claim of easy access raises significant regulatory and health concerns.

In response to an SBS Thai query, a Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) spokesperson said: "It is not legal to import GLP-1 medicines or peptide products into Australia for commercial purposes without appropriate authorisation and declaration."

The spokesperson said GLP-1 receptor agonists, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are prescription-only medicines in Australia and should be used under the supervision of a qualified health professional.

The regulator has also warned about unregistered products being sold as GLP-1 medicines, particularly those obtained online or from overseas.

In March, TGA testing found several imported products labelled as containing GLP-1 or GLP-1 analogues contained none of those ingredients. The regulator advised consumers to obtain prescription medicines from registered Australian pharmacies rather than social media or other digital platforms.

The regulator has also increased its focus on unapproved peptide products.

Earlier this month, with assistance from NSW Police, the TGA seized more than $120,000 worth of unapproved peptide and anabolic steroid products from two NSW properties. The TGA said the products had allegedly been imported, relabelled and promoted for sale through social media and a website.

One of the products seized was labelled "retatrutide" — a name that also appeared in SBS Thai's investigation.

We found retatrutide offered at $300 for a 10mg vial at a Thai grocery store in Geelong, Victoria. The seller claimed the injectable product could help with weight loss and work similarly to other GLP-1 medicines.

A poster at a Thai grocery store in Victoria reads: "Weight loss injections and citizenship mock tests available here." Source: SBS News / Atitaya Teepawat

Retatrutide is different from approved GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy. While those medicines contain semaglutide, retatrutide is an experimental drug that acts on three hormone pathways involved in appetite and metabolism. It is not approved for sale as a medicine in Australia.

SBS Thai did not independently test the product or establish what was inside the vial. The TGA says unapproved peptide products have not been evaluated for safety, quality or effectiveness.

There is also a separate health warning involving products labelled retatrutide.

In June, Victoria's Department of Health said it had been notified of six cases of acute liver injury since January among people who had used products labelled as retatrutide. The department said investigations were continuing.

Demand is surging

The informal market is emerging alongside a rapid increase in legitimate use of GLP-1 medicines.

Researchers at UNSW found that total sales of GLP-1 medicines rose from about 58,000 in May 2020 to 500,000 in April 2025. They also noted a significant disruption in sales from late 2022 to early 2024, when a drug shortage caused sales to drop by almost 80 per cent.

The researchers found that private, non-subsidised access had grown sharply, accounting for 43.8 per cent of estimated use by April 2025, with prices up to $600 per month.

The study did not include Wegovy and Saxenda, which are marketed specifically for weight loss. The researchers said their figures should therefore be regarded as a minimum estimate of overall GLP-1 use.

Source: SBS News

That expanding market is also being discussed heavily on social media.

Like Darwan, Ople Petchdee, who lives in Croydon South in Melbourne's east, also bought a GLP-1 injectable from a beauty clinic just outside the Thai capital, Bangkok.

Petchdee, who has called Australia home for the past 15 years, says she became interested in the medicines after seeing friends post about their experiences.

"Everyone posted on their Facebook, on their social media, that these medications helped them lose weight. So, my friends suggested I use them, too," she tells SBS Thai.

Beyond the weight-loss promise

For Trevor Steward, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Melbourne, the concern is not only how people obtain GLP-1 medicines but also how the drugs are presented and understood online.

Associate professor Trevor Steward is running a clinical trial examining how GLP-1 drugs affect the neurobiological function of people with eating disorders. Source: Supplied / Trevor Steward

Steward is currently running a clinical trial examining how GLP-1 drugs affect the neurobiological function of people with binge eating disorder.

It's not about aesthetics. It's not about achieving a certain number on a scale.

"It's about someone's mental and physical wellbeing. And that's something that needs to be considered holistically with a doctor involved," Steward tells SBS Thai.

He says there are also unanswered questions about what happens when treatment stops for people with eating disorders.

"If the weight comes back, we can maybe stipulate that the food noise will come back. And how will that person cope with that, thinking that they have achieved a certain sense of recovery and then falling back into that old pattern of behaviour before."

Steward says social media often strips away that nuance, framing GLP-1 medicines as a shortcut to achieving a particular body shape or weight, rather than treating them as serious medications to be considered in the context of a person's overall mental and physical health.

For Darwan, who had gone looking for a way to lose weight, reality was harder.

"My mood was depressing. I suffered from energy loss."

I will not use [GLP-1 drugs] again.

title: One Nation MP admits the party's true migration target 'isn't too different' from Labor's
text:
in brief Pauline Hanson has rejected claims on immigration made by her own MP.

David Farley conceded the party's overall intake numbers are not too different from Labor's forecasts.

One Nation's immigration stance is under question after an MP said the party would include an extra 100,000 people annually in its policy — bringing its target total higher than present forecasts under Labor.

Farrer MP David Farley, who clinched Sussan Ley's old seat from the Coalition at a by-election, told the ABC Insiders program on Sunday morning that his party had decided to separate a "true NOM", or net overseas migration figure, from certain other categories of migrants.

However, party leader Pauline Hanson was forced to quickly intervene, refuting the claims just hours later on social media. Party policy is to "cut net overseas migration to 130,000".

"One Nation's target is less than half of Labor's current level," she wrote.

This contradicts messaging from Farley, who said One Nation's stated policy of getting net overseas migration down to 130,000 excluded people brought in under a Pacific scheme, aged-care nurses and other in-demand skilled workers.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Adding those groups would amount to an additional 100,000 arrivals, bringing the total to 230,000 — 5,000 more than the budget forecast of 225,000 in the coming four years.

"What we're doing is we're focusing on the NOM in its true form, and then we've got these programs that have been available now for over a decade that drive our economy," Farley told Insiders.

"The raw number is not too different, but the reality is, where do we need them?

"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."

One Nation 'effectively backing' Labor's plan

The comments come as public debate continues around the optimum level of migration to Australia.

Net overseas migration dropped to 306,000 in 2024-25, brought down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000 under Liberal-National government policy.

Cabinet minister Chris Bowen said net overseas migration could not just be redefined.

"My overwhelming conclusion was he's pretty comfortable with what the government's doing," Bowen told reporters.

"I'm not sure what campaign One Nation's going to run on migration if they're effectively backing in what the Albanese government is doing."

Opposition immigration spokesman Jonno Duniam said voters were owed a clear explanation of what the party's immigration policy actually is.

"These are not semantic distinctions. They have real consequences for housing, infrastructure, essential services, wages, jobs and the economy," he said.

"For a party that has spent years telling Australians it has all the answers on immigration, One Nation is having extraordinary difficulty answering the most basic question of all: how many migrants would actually come to Australia under its policy."

Opinion polls have shown that voters trust One Nation to manage migration better than the two major parties.

Hanson says One Nation's cuts will come from "fewer international students and dependants, a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants, and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs".

David Farley won One Nation's first lower house seat in the Farrer by-election in May, securing an unprecedented 32.9 percent swing. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

"Short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration," she wrote.

Individuals must stay in Australia for 12 months in a 16-month period to be included in NOM figures, meaning short-term seasonal workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme are typically not counted.

Long-term workers on the same scheme are counted, as are backpakers and working holiday makers who typically stay in the country for more than a year.

Hanson will test racial discrimination laws in the High Court.

The confusion comes as Hanson declared she would take her racial discrimination challenge with Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi to the High Court.

The senator lost a Federal Court appeal last month against a ruling which found her in breach of racial vilification laws after she told the Greens senator to "piss off back to Pakistan".

Asked if racial discrimination laws should be changed, Farley said he wasn't convinced they should be.

He said his leader's comments "can be taken as an insult" but weren't inciting racial discrimination.

"Hanson's got every right to challenge it," Farley said.

"I think if we went through the pub test, I know which way it would go. It'd go in Pauline's favour."

This is the second time Hanson has had to correct comments made by Farley after he said he would display both the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags alongside the Australian flag at his electorate office.

One Nation's policy is to only fly the Australian flag on public buildings. Hanson has described having multiple official flags as "extremely divisive".

title: 'We support the club': Sydney Swans' fans stay loyal amid scandal engulfing men’s side
text:
In brief The Sydney Swans have played their first game since being rocked by a sexual assault scandal.

A planned walk out of the men's game proved more of a trickle than a mass exodus.

The Sydney Swans AFLW team has set a new attendance record, with fans warmly welcoming them to the field despite a major sexual assault scandal engulfing the men's side.

Attendance reached 16,672 spectators on Sunday afternoon, a new record for the women's club which more than doubles the previous record of 8,264.

The Swans AFLW team played their second-ever game at the Sydney Cricket Ground (SCG) on Sunday in a history double-header before the men took to the field.

A planned mass walk-out of fans ahead of the men's match failed to materialise as large crowds remained for both games. A small stream of supporters, some waving placards, did exit the SCG prior to the men's game, various media reported.

Five Swans players, including elite players Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner, have been suspended for the remainder of the AFL season for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

No one has been arrested or charged, as Sex Crimes Squad detectives continue to investigate.

Several fans told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency that they still supported the club despite feeling disappointed in players involved in the scandal.

"We support the club wholeheartedly," Swans supporter Russell Le-Guier said.

"The club itself is what this is about, not the individual players, they'll come and go over the years, but it's the club itself that we support."

The Swans AFLW team doubled their crowd attendance record during only their second time playing at the SCG. Source: Getty / Cameron Spencer

Sydney Swans Chairman Andrew Pridham said: "The five players made a terrible mistake."

"However, they are part of our club, and as such we will do everything in our power to care for them," he said during a pre-game event.

"We do not excuse their behaviour. We do not ignore the impact it has had on so many people — and in particular women."

Don't punish the other players, fans say

Speaking with AAP, several fans said they were supportive of the men on the field.

Rosalie Le-Guier said she'd be cheering just as loud, if not louder than usual, when the men took the field.

"You don't punish the boys in the rest of the team," she said.

"We're here to support the club. We're here to support the rest of the players."

Another Swans fan, Kate Hipsley said she wouldn't be walking out of the stadium.

"As far as we know, the men playing in the men's game have not done anything wrong and they will be hurting as well," she said.

"I don't care about the premiership — it's more important than premierships — you care for the culture of the team, which has taken a huge hit."

Supporter David McGilchrist said he was generally happy with how the club had dealt with the scandal, despite being disappointed.

"I'm disappointed, and I've got a bit of anger now as well of what's happened, but a lot of disappointment and massive shock," he said.

"But I'm here to support the girls, the men, the club."

'Healing and moving forward'

Pridham said the club intends to rebuild trust in the community.

"While we are deeply shocked and disappointed with what transpired, we believe that since it occurred, we have acted with honesty, dignity and urgency," he said.

"Now we begin the process of healing and moving forward."

That will involve a better understanding of "how our cultural pillars failed to prevent such a thing from happening", he elaborated.

Investigation continues

Three women at the centre of the alleged sexual assault scandal have not spoken publicly as they consider potential civil claims.

It's understood the women joined players at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel after the Swans' win over Essendon last Sunday night.

One of the trio, who has engaged personal injury specialists Slater and Gordon, was navigating an "incredibly traumatic experience", according to senior attorney Jackson Pannam.

He says the firm has been asked to determine whether the woman, who has put multiple sexual assault allegations to police, has grounds to file a civil claim.

Pannam said the woman contacted police immediately after the alleged assaults and that her world had been turned upside down.

title: Axed by Abbott, backed by crowdfunders: How Amanda McKenzie keeps finding hope in a crisis
text:
From tech-platform shutdowns to defining national moments, the climate chief shares how public anger outpaced government policy – and how there is enormous power in telling better stories.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Amanda McKenzie – climate wunderkind, activist for hope and Climate Council chief executive – and her husband and two young children came down with COVID-19 recently, she got out the roller skates. She and her husband unearthed some jigsaw puzzles, turned their living room into a makeshift roller rink, and told the kids to have fun. Then, they went back to work in their home office. As she tells this story over lunch, I’m struck by two things. First, it says a lot about their commitment to community that McKenzie and her husband chose to lock down their family at home for a week, regardless of whether they were still symptomatic. And second: living in McKenzie’s house sounds like a hoot. We’re meeting at Patsy’s, a tranquil up-market vegetarian wine bar in Melbourne’s inner north, where almost all the produce prepared in the kitchen is grown in the owner’s regenerative farm in Victoria’s Central Highlands. McKenzie has nominated this lunch spot, which seems an almost too-perfect choice to interview one of the most senior women in Australia’s environment movement.

Advertisement

Zucchini flowers with almond crema and salsa al dragoncello at Patsy’s. Ruby Alexander “I’m quite a utilitarian eater, but my husband has a very bougie, foodie vibe, so he’s made me more of a foodie,” she says. “I think if I was just left to my own devices, I’d be just eating a salad … premixed leaves with sun-dried tomatoes or something.” Today, McKenzie eschews wine in favour of a pot of English breakfast tea, while I order a hibiscus spritz mocktail. It is a bougie wine bar, after all. McKenzie has lived almost half her life in the public eye, although she isn’t necessarily a household name outside environment circles. Her first leadership role came 20 years ago when, aged 23, she co-founded the Australian Youth Climate Coalition with fellow law graduate Anna Rose. The pair hit the ground running, growing a fledgling coalition of 27 youth groups to a national organisation numbering 100,000 members three years later. Anna Rose (left) and Amanda McKenzie pictured at their offices in Sydney in 2009. Peter Rae Back then, as she travelled around organising meetings and strategic campaigns, McKenzie often found herself the only woman in the room. There were many who underestimated this young woman and the importance of the message she was trying to convey.

Advertisement

“At that time, it was a ‘future issue’,” she says. “I talked about [the impacts on our] kids and grandchildren, and it strikes me now, these kids I was talking about 20 years ago, they’re here: they’re eight and five, and experiencing the impacts already.” Related Article Antarctica ‘It’s beginning to look a lot like the future’: Fears over sudden loss of sea ice Without intending to, it was former prime minister Tony Abbott who lit the fuse that propelled McKenzie into making her life’s mission the fight against climate change. In 2011, she joined the fledgling Australian Climate Commission as a senior communications adviser, determined to shift public debate on Australia’s changing climate. The commission was established by former prime minister Julia Gillard and led by Professor Tim Flannery. It was designed to provide independent advice on the science of climate change, and was announced as public alarm grew about climate change, fuelled by back-to-back La Nina weather events, and on the heels of the 1997-2010 millennium drought.

Advertisement

In its first report to government, The Critical Decade, commissioners warned that climate change “risks have never been clearer, and the case for action has never been more urgent”. Julia Gillard, then prime minister, received the first Australian Climate Commission report from chief Tim Flannery (left) and report author Will Steffen at Parliament House in 2011. Andrew Meares Less than two weeks after the Coalition came to power two years later, the commission’s time was up. In one of his first acts as environment minister, Greg Hunt phoned Flannery to tell him the commission would be axed, as part of the Abbott government’s commitment to scrap the carbon tax. “So very quietly, I’d just gone to the commissioners and said, ‘if we started a new thing, would you be up for it?’ And Tim Flannery was like, ‘Yes, let’s do it!’” After Hunt’s announcement, the commission issued a “relatively neutral response”, McKenzie says, stressing the importance of science to Australian democracy. Flannery held a press conference in which he praised Hunt’s “gracious” conduct in their conversation. Four days later, they officially launched The Climate Council, with founding commissioners including Flannery, the late Professor Will Steffen, Professor Veena Sahajwalla, Gerry Hueston and Professor Lesley Hughes.

Advertisement

“It just went crazy, as soon as it hit the media in the morning,” McKenzie says. “We did a bunch of radio, we started to do some TV news. Some of the newspapers had it. And then it started this big viral moment crowdfunding campaign. Professor Will Steffen addressing the media during a doorstop interview at Parliament House in Canberra in 2013. Alex Ellinghausen “Within that first day, we raised $500,000 and by the end of the day, Twitter [now X] thought we were buying followers, so they shut us down. PayPal thought we were money-laundering, so they shut us down because we’d raised money so fast ... It was this cyclone of activity.” They raised $1.3 million within the first week – more than the previous Climate Commission’s budget – from more than 15,000 people for whom Abbott’s cuts to climate commitments felt like attacks on science. Since then, the principle that “we should base our democratic debate on evidence”, as McKenzie puts it, has driven the way the Climate Council operates. Another element of the Climate Council’s approach is something akin to intentional hope.

title: The genius of Dolly Parton, the last great unifier in a divided nation
text:
Advertisement

CultureMusicVale Opinion The genius of Dolly Parton, the last great unifier in a divided nation Cory Alpert Former White House staffer August 26, 2026 — 11:39am

August 26, 2026 — 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The machinery of American politics sorts everything that it sees. Every moment becomes a litmus test, where every cultural symbol is judged as either MAGA or its opposite. Artists, companies, cities, sports, and even beer get assigned into these categories. A political age consumes everything it touches. Dolly Parton was one of the last major exceptions. Photo: Marija Ercegovac She managed a high-wire act of being entirely herself, a vision of American individualism done right, a preacher who could build a congregation without demanding conversion – where its members could briefly see a piece of shared humanity in each other in their shared appreciation of the woman we Americans knew as Saint Dolly.

Advertisement

Her first big break on the country music stage was as the “singing girl” on The Porter Wagoner Show. During her first performance, the audience booed her during the commercial break. They were angry at the change that this brash, blonde starlet with an unusual voice represented. Related Article Vale Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 The show allowed her star to rise, and eventually she set out on her own. Her break with Wagoner, then the kingmaker of country music, is what inspired Dolly to write I Will Always Love You. It’s a song about leaving someone you love but refusing to hate the person you’re leaving behind. The way that Dolly left Porter became the blueprint for a career as the last great unifier in American politics. Later in her life, when Porter was left poor at the end of his career, she bought his music catalogue and gifted it back to him. By the time she built her empire, she understood how fragile the kind of fame she had developed could be. In her flock were conservatives and liberals, evangelicals and atheists, drag queens and NASCAR drivers.

Advertisement

Gallery Gallery icon 7 images Vale Dolly Parton in Australia All the while, she refused to endorse anything while embracing everyone. Some of that instinct had been trained into her by country music’s famously possessive fans. When Dolly crossed into pop, she told TV talkshow host Larry King that she was worried that she was leaving those fans behind. But she told them that she wasn’t leaving country music. She was taking it with her. For many artists, that act would feel like cowardice, to never state your beliefs – to just shut up and sing. But Dolly Parton was anything but a coward. Instead, she was fearless about defining herself and refused to define anyone else.

Advertisement

In a 1984 interview with Andy Warhol, the painter told her that she could be a great preacher. She replied, “What do you mean? I am a great preacher.” Related Article Vale Dolly Parton wrote more than 3000 songs – but we’ve picked her top 10 What she preached was nothing short of American individualism done right. The internet today is flooded with her quotes and Dollyisms, using her very body to grant permission for her fans to become whatever ambitious, sequinned thing they are capable of becoming. Her only demand in return for that permission was to afford everyone else the same privilege. In the same interview, she talked about being a star, as finding your own place and shining within it. It does not require a big stage or a big wig. In Dolly’s universe, there was room enough for everyone to shine. Where I grew up in the rural South, imagination could often be hard to come by. Our school system was so underfunded that parts of it became known as the Corridor of Shame.

Advertisement

It’s the same world that Dolly grew up in. Her father couldn’t read, and the hard, patient life of the mountains of East Tennessee did not afford much possibility beyond those hills. Related Article Vale Beyond the wigs, there was always Dolly Parton’s wondrous wit and wisdom As Dolly’s star grew, she sent that possibility back. She sent books to every child in her home county until they were five years old. The program slowly expanded across the South, then across America. Last year, the Imagination Library delivered its 2 millionth book in Australia alone. Across the world, more than 300 million kids have gotten books – for many, it was the only way they would receive them. She was giving children the resources to decide who they might become. America often mistakes individualism for abandonment. The version that Dolly preached was that each of our lives belong to us, but she could give us each something that could make it larger.

Advertisement

Faith without works is dead, after all. The congregation of Dolly does not agree on every point. Dolly became the great unifier by creating a church big enough for everyone to find room for themselves. To love Dolly was to stand alongside people with whom you share little, and to understand that they have as much right to their place as you do. Dolly gave all of us a place where we could be different together. Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

title: Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyMiddle East at war Opinion Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard August 26, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump administration is hallucinating again. The United States’ “economic D-Day” against Iran will exhaust political consent in Washington for this ill-conceived war long before it forces Iran’s Revolutionary Guard to capitulate. It draws out the spectacle of Donald Trump’s aimless flailing in a region that neither he nor his close advisers begin to understand, further convulsing the global energy, food and commodity markets and further eviscerating US strategic credibility. Even if Trump turns the dial up to 11, he may not get the response that he wants. AP The plan to mount the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary” requires also mobilising China, Russia, India, Turkey, a resentful Europe and the world’s major financial centres in a joint campaign to throttle Iran, a country that has already learned to live with 2200 separate US sanctions. The US Treasury could plausibly have pulled off such a feat 10 to 15 years ago, when it was able to crush nations by the “boa constrictor” method, using all the tools of the world’s dollarised financial system. But that supremacy relied on a tight-knit phalanx of democratic allies – or what we used to call the West. Such a world no longer exists, and China cannot be pushed around any longer.

Advertisement

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened the economic obliteration of any country that declines to enlist as foot soldiers in America’s quarrel. “If you insist on doing business with them – either transferring money, buying their oil, doing seaborne ship transport – the US government will put its full might and force toward enforcing against you,” he said. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war The White House says this is the Iran endgame. We’ve heard that before Such hubris is courting fate for a nation that depends on constant inflows of capital from these same countries to fund its twin deficits and that already has to pay punitive interest rates to sell its bonds. The US Treasury made a Faustian pact by issuing so much short-term debt. The trap is closing. Bessent must roll over or fund almost $US6 trillion ($8.4 trillion) every three months in a hostile market. The budget deficit was $US432 billion for the single month of July, up 48 per cent from the year before.

Advertisement

Trump has a solution for this and a warning for any bond investor who declines to feed his appetite. “We have many types of intervention. The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will,” he said. Does he intend to parachute the 101st Airborne into London’s Canary Wharf and Singapore’s harbour district to cart off pension fund managers in shackles for interrogation at Guantanamo? The move draws out the spectacle of Donald Trump’s aimless flailing in a region that neither he nor his close advisers begin to understand, further convulsing the global energy, food and commodity markets. AP It is normal to dial up pressure by starting with economic sanctions before escalating to killing people. Everybody can see that Trump is doing it the other way round because killing has comprehensively failed. The world can see that the US is overstretched, lacks sufficient military power to enforce its will, has exhausted two-thirds of its Patriot interceptors and “virtually all” its surface-to-surface (ATACMS) missiles, and has denuded its defences in the Far East. It can see that the US lacks the stomach for a full ground invasion of Iran and anything short of that is whistling in the wind.

Advertisement

Iran can see all of this too. The regime has survived a bombing campaign and the assassination of 180 members of its leadership. Sanctions are almost laughable at this juncture. Related Article Middle East at war US military top brass dispatched to aircraft carrier rocked by talk of crumbling morale Iran’s land border stretches for 5900 kilometres across seven countries, most of them either friendly or cynically transactional. The frontier rises in an arc from Pakistan to the Eurasian heartland around the Caspian Sea, then down the other side to Turkey and the entire eastern side of Iraq. It is impossible to sustain a goods blockade. The International North-South Transport Corridor already runs as a rail freight link from Russia through Central Asia to Iran. The maritime route via the Caspian does a booming trade as well. Russia cannot export much grain through the Black Sea right now because of Ukrainian drones, so it is exporting what it can to Iran and through Iranian proxies to the wider Middle East. Ergo, a) Iran will have enough food for itself even if its economy is in dire straits and b) Iran will gain strategic leverage as a grain conduit to a region facing serious food stress.

Advertisement

China currently buys 90 per cent of Iran’s oil and in return China sells it machinery, vehicles and electronics, including sensors and engines for Iran’s Shahed drones as well as propellants for its ballistic missiles. China will not let the US dictate how and with whom it may trade. It has gone to some lengths to demonstrate this objection. The world knows that an overstretched America lacks the capability and stomach for a full invasion of Iran. Getty Images If Washington imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese banks and entities, Beijing has a rich menu of retaliation, starting with curbs on critical minerals. Bessent has demonstrated by his actions that he fears rising US bond yields. Beijing knows this, and if it wants to rattle his cage, it can play a few hedge fund tricks of its own by weaponising $US4 trillion of dollar assets held by the Chinese central bank, the state-controlled commercial banks and the giant state-policy banks.

Advertisement

If the US does impose secondary sanctions on Chinese banks, it will have to do the same to European banks that do business with China, otherwise the financial blockade breaks down. But the European Union now has its blocking statute aimed at forbidding its own companies from complying with US extraterritorial sanctions or submitting to US coercion. Iran has a say in the matter too and may choose to hold Trump’s feet to the fire, exploiting the window between now and the midterm elections to cause commodity havoc while always staying just below the threshold of total conflagration. It is normal to dial up pressure by starting with economic sanctions before escalating to killing people. Everybody can see that Trump is doing it the other way round because killing has comprehensively failed. “If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf,” said Mohsen Rezaee, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. That too is bluster, but it is closer to the truth than the US cares to admit. Iran still controls the Strait of Hormuz and has a second partial stranglehold over the Red Sea via its Houthi allies.

Advertisement

It still has a sufficient arsenal of drones and missiles hidden in mountains to strike commercial shipping at will and enough to inflict serious damage to the energy infrastructure of the Gulf states. The rest of us are condemned to months of mounting stress in the global hydrocarbon markets as storage falls to critically low levels and even greater stress in the markets for diesel, petrol and jet fuel. Despite Trump’s assertions, Iran still controls the Strait of Hormuz. Getty Images The refined petroleum products that we consume are trading today at levels equivalent to crude oil prices of $US140 to $US160 a barrel. The IATA jet fuel index is $US170 in Europe and $US165 in the US.

Advertisement

Wholesale diesel costs $US185 in New York harbour and $US180 in Rotterdam, and it is diesel that fuels farming, trucking, construction and swaths of the industrial economy on both sides of the Atlantic. Natural gas prices in Europe are trading this week at €69 ($112) per megawatt-hour, higher than the panic peak at the onset of Trump’s Iran war. European inventories are disturbingly low for this time of the year, and Britain has almost no safety buffer. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will face his first big crisis if this northern winter proves harsh. These commodity costs are becoming embedded in the global supply chain, are already visible in rising bond yields and will soon be visible in rising inflation and the cost of living. It is hard to see any way out of this impasse, since Trump has only two options: either to accept defeat on Iranian terms, which become more exigent by the week, or to mobilise the US for a long, bloody and costly war that consumes his presidency and may also end in defeat. He shrinks from both.

Manhattan Gold Corporation has delivered another round of strong, broad gold intercepts from its Jaws prospect in Nunavut, Canada, with drilling extending the known mineralised system by more than 150 metres to the southwest. The latest results from the company’s maiden drill campaign at its Hook Lake project include a significant 25.9-metre hit grading 1.59 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 89.92m, which housed a richer 6.1-metre core at 3.62g/t gold. This follows on from the stunning interval announced last week of 41.15 metres running at 4.66g/t gold from just 83.82m downhole at the project. Manhattan Gold’s Hook Lake project area in Nunavut, Canada. Other notable intersections from this second batch of assays included 35.05m at 1.23g/t gold from 124.97m, with a 9.14-metre slice of 2.52g/t, and 22.86m at 2.37g/t gold from a shallower 74.68m. The latter intercept contained a particularly spicy 1.52-metre section grading a hefty 26.8g/t gold. The results land at a time when Canada’s vast northern territory of Nunavut is proving to be a hot address for gold explorers. Home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast and one of Canada’s largest gold mines, peers such as B2Gold and Fury Gold Mines are also advancing programs, underlining the district-scale appetite for new ounces. With the gold price recently pushing higher to more than US$4600 (A$6400) per ounce, any exploration success is getting a serious second look from the market.

Advertisement

‘The Jaws system remains open along strike and at depth.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard Manhattan says the latest intercepts from its Jaws target are returning thicker, higher-grade results than those recorded in nearby historic drilling from 1988, suggesting the company’s modern exploration approach is already paying dividends and adding material upside to the historical data. Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard said:“Drilling at Jaws continues to deliver multiple broad gold zones with higher grade internal cores, led by 25.90 metres at 1.59g/t gold. Drill results including JWS26005 and JWS26006, also highlight the material upside compared to historic drilling by revealing thicker and higher-grade intercepts when compared to the nearest 1988 drillholes.” Jaws, the most advanced target at Hook Lake, hosts a non-JORC foreign estimate of 3.4 million tonnes at 2.38g/t gold for 285,000 ounces of gold, defined by drilling in the late 1980’s. Manhattan’s current program has been designed to confirm and potentially expand on that historic work. Notably, the company’s work has also recalibrated the geological map. Manhattan says its new drilling has shifted the interpreted position of the gold-bearing main shear zone 20m to 30m northwest of where historic records had placed it, providing the company with a sharper geological model for follow-up drilling. The revised geometry of the orebody provides a much stronger basis for follow-up drill targeting and may open up previously under-explored zones.

Advertisement

With the rods still turning at Jaws, Manhattan is looking at a bigger picture for the deposit. The company has assays pending for a further 12 drillholes, including a key hole that tested below the footprint of all historic drilling at Jaws, opening up the possibility for new mineralisation lurking below. The pending results also include the first-ever drill tests of the company’s Spectre and Lotus prospects. Spectre is a high-grade volcanogenic massive sulphide target where historic drilling in 1974 returned impressive polymetallic hits including 10.51 metres at 2.91 per cent copper, 6.70 per cent zinc, 95.67g/t silver and 1.04g/t gold. The Lotus prospect, described as a “Jaws-style” gold target, has never been drilled despite rock chip sampling in 2025 returning high-grade results of 8.01g/t gold and 2660g/t silver. With drilling at Jaws continuing to deliver broad zones of gold, a historic resource to build upon and a pipeline of assays from both extension and new discovery targets, Manhattan doesn’t look short of catalysts. As the company continues to piece together the puzzle at Hook Lake, punters will likely be watching closely for what the drill bit uncovers next. Holland House in Sydney’s Middle Cove was as famous for its architecture as it was for a ballet performed on the cantilevered terrace that hovers 12 metres above rock and bush. The balcony had no handrails.
